text: Ecuador president removed as head of ruling party as feud deepens. QUITO (Reuters) - Ecuador's ruling Country Alliance party, founded by former president Rafael Correa over a decade ago, has removed President Lenin Moreno as its head, citing repeated failures in leadership, as a schism between the former allies deepens. The Country Alliance party, which has been divided by the two politicians, late on Tuesday announced that Correa ally Ricardo Patino, a former foreign minister, would replace Moreno as party leader. The head of the national Country Alliance party has unanimously decided, it said in a statement announcing the immediate removal of Lenin Moreno as president of the Country Alliance party. Ecuador's government, however, said it did not recognize the decision and stressed Moreno remained the head of the party. "Country Alliance is a political party, not an estate ... These actions are wrong and do not reflect the feeling of our political base," acting vice president Alejandra Vicuna told journalists on Tuesday. Moreno, a Correa protégé who previously served as his vice president, was elected earlier this year to succeed the fiery leftist. At the time, opposition critics warned Moreno would be a puppet of political heavyweight Correa, whom they accused of seeking to stage a presidential comeback in 2021. But Moreno, a paraplegic former United Nations special envoy on disability, has quickly broken with Correa, who is now living abroad, in his wife's home country of Belgium. Moreno, who is seeking presidential term limits via a referendum to revise the constitution, has sidelined another top Correa ally from the vice presidency and is overseeing a corruption probe that has ensnared former high-level officials. Vicuna replaced Jorge Glas, who was also Correa's vice president, after Glas came under investigation in a corruption scandal centered on Brazilian construction company Odebrecht. He is currently in jail. Polls indicate Moreno has widespread popular support in Ecuador. His approval levels have jumped from around 66 percent in May, when he was sworn in, to about 77 percent in September, a recent survey by local pollster Cedatos showed. Many Ecuadoreans report being satisfied with his attempts to investigate corruption and boost social welfare. His conciliatory temperament is also welcomed by some who were tired of Correa's confrontational style.

text: House Speaker Ryan states that work remains to secure freedom in Cuba. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Paul Ryan indicated on Saturday that even after Fidel Castro's death, "much work remains to secure the freedom of the Cuban people," emphasizing the need for the United States to be fully committed to this cause. "Now that Fidel Castro is dead, the cruelty and oppression of his regime should die with him," Ryan stated. "Today let us reflect on the memory and sacrifices of all those who have suffered under the Castros."

text: Clinton loses to Sanders in coal state of West Virginia. WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - U.S. Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders defeated Hillary Clinton on Tuesday in West Virginia’s primary, winning over voters who are skeptical about the economy and indicating potential challenges Clinton may face in industrial states during the general election. The loss slows Clinton’s path to the nomination, although she remains favored to become the Democratic candidate in the Nov. 8 election. In a November match-up with Donald Trump, Clinton will need to gain the support of working-class voters in the U.S. Rust Belt, which includes key states such as Ohio and Pennsylvania. Trump, 69, won contests in West Virginia and Nebraska on Tuesday. The presumptive Republican nominee is scheduled to meet with party leaders in the U.S. Congress on Thursday, including U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Paul Ryan. After Ryan indicated last week that he was not yet ready to endorse Trump, Trump stated on Sunday that he would have to decide whether he still wanted Ryan to preside over the party’s July convention. Trump expressed in a Fox interview on Tuesday night that he would like Ryan to chair the convention as planned, describing him as a good man who wants what is good for the party. Trump has focused on Clinton’s extended contest with Sanders, a 74-year-old U.S. senator from Vermont, and has criticized her for not securing a decisive win over Sanders, her only rival for the Democratic Party’s nomination since Feb. 1. Clinton, 68, has indicated that she will disregard Trump’s personal insults, including his repeated use of the nickname “Crooked Hillary,” and will instead address his policy statements. Concerns about the economy were significant in West Virginia’s Democratic primary, with approximately six in 10 voters expressing serious worries about the direction of the U.S. economy in the coming years. The same percentage identified the economy and jobs as their primary voting issue, according to a preliminary ABC News exit poll. A remark made by Clinton at an Ohio town hall in March, suggesting that the country would “put a lot of coal miners and coal companies out of business,” may have negatively impacted her standing with voters in coal-mining states such as West Virginia. During her visit to West Virginia and Ohio last week, Clinton apologized to displaced coal and steel workers for her remark, which she stated had been taken out of context, and discussed her plan to assist in retraining coal workers for clean energy jobs. To secure the Democratic nomination, a candidate requires 2,383 delegates. Entering West Virginia, Clinton, a former U.S. secretary of state, had 2,228 delegates, including 523 superdelegates, who are party members free to support any candidate. Sanders had 1,454 delegates, including 39 superdelegates. An additional 29 delegates will be allocated based on West Virginia’s results. Clinton and Sanders are set to compete in another primary contest on May 17. Both candidates are also preparing for the June 7 contests, the final events in the lengthy nominating season, in which nearly 700 delegates are at stake, including 475 in California, where Sanders is currently focusing his efforts. Sanders has committed to continuing his campaign through the Democrats’ July 25-28 convention in Philadelphia, seeking input in shaping the party’s platform. Sanders has informed supporters at rallies that most opinion polls suggest he would have a greater chance of defeating Trump in a general election match-up compared to Clinton. Trump, transitioning into general election mode, has begun considering potential running mates, stating on Fox Tuesday night that he has narrowed his list to five individuals. He did not exclude the possibility of selecting New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a former rival who ended his presidential campaign in February. Christie, who endorsed Trump and subsequently campaigned for him, was mentioned on Monday.

text: Obama, Putin discuss Syria and Ukraine in brief summit meeting. LIMA (Reuters) - U.S. President Barack Obama and Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke for approximately four minutes on Sunday at the APEC summit regarding Syria and Ukraine, in what is anticipated to be their final in-person meeting before Obama departs from office. The two leaders met at the outset of the summit in Lima, the capital of Peru. They exchanged pleasantries and remained standing during their conversation. Obama later stated at a news conference that he expressed to Putin the U.S. concern about the bloodshed and chaos in Syria “sown by constant bombing attacks” by both the Syrian and Russian militaries, emphasizing the need for a ceasefire and political transition. “As usual I was candid and courteous but very clear about the strong differences we have on policy,” Obama remarked. Putin, during a separate news conference, expressed gratitude to Obama for the years of joint work during their meeting in Lima. “I told him that we would be happy to see him (Obama) in Russia anytime if he wants, can and has desire,” Putin stated. The relationship between Obama and Putin has been described as challenging. Last week, the U.S. president noted that he had warned Putin about potential consequences for cyber attacks attributed to Moscow, which were perceived as attempts to influence the U.S. election. Obama also urged President Putin to assist in the implementation of the Minsk peace agreement by collaborating with France, Germany, Ukraine, and the United States to cease the conflict in the Donbass region of Ukraine. During his campaign for the presidency, Republican President-elect Donald Trump praised Putin. On Sunday, Putin indicated that Trump had confirmed his willingness to improve relations.

text: Russian long-range bombers strike Islamic State targets in Syria. MOSCOW (Reuters) - Six Russian long-range bombers targeted Islamic State positions near the town of Albu Kamal in Syria's Deir al-Zor Province on Wednesday, according to a statement from the Russian Defence Ministry. The TU-22M3 bombers departed from bases in Russia, traveling over Iran and Iraq before executing the strike, the ministry reported. The statement indicated that the aircraft targeted Islamic State supply depots, militants, and armored vehicles, with satellite and drone surveillance confirming the destruction of all designated targets. Additionally, Sukhoi-30SM fighter jets, operating from the Hmeymim air base in Syria, provided escort for the bombers during their mission in Syrian airspace, and all aircraft returned safely to their bases. On Tuesday, Russia accused the United States of effectively providing cover for Islamic State units in Syria and suggested that the U.S. was only nominally engaged in combating terrorism in the Middle East. The Russian Defence Ministry specifically claimed that the U.S. air force had attempted to obstruct Russian strikes on Islamic State fighters near Albu Kamal. In response to these allegations, Colonel Ryan Dillon, a spokesperson for the U.S.-led coalition against Islamic State, remarked that the statements from the Russian Ministry of Defense are comparable in accuracy to their air campaign, describing this as a reason for Russia to continue issuing what he termed as their latest barrage of falsehoods.

text: Florida mayors press presidential debate moderators for climate airtime. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Mayors of 21 cities in Florida on Friday requested that the moderators of the upcoming presidential debates in Miami pose questions to candidates regarding their plans to address rising sea levels attributed to climate change, a significant concern for the state's coastal communities. “It would be unconscionable for these issues of grave concern for the people of Florida to not be addressed in the upcoming debate you will be hosting in the state,” the mayors stated in a letter to CNN, The Washington Post, Univision, and other media outlets hosting the Democratic and Republican debates scheduled for March 9 and March 10 in Miami. The bipartisan group of mayors, representing coastal cities and towns from Miami to Tampa, expressed dissatisfaction that climate change has not been discussed in the numerous televised debates held so far. Among the four remaining Republican candidates, none have indicated that they support measures to address climate change, with all advocating for a reduction in federal environmental regulations. One of the letter’s signatories, Pinecrest Mayor Cindy Lerner, traveled to New Hampshire in February to urge Florida Republican candidate Senator Marco Rubio to engage on this topic. Rubio has remarked that the climate has always been changing and that he will not endorse policies aimed at combating climate change that could harm the economy. Billionaire businessman Donald Trump has described climate change as a conspiracy created by China, while Texas Senator Ted Cruz referred to climate science as a “pseudoscientific theory.” Ohio Governor John Kasich acknowledged climate change as a concern but has not proposed a solution to address it. Democratic candidates Hillary Clinton and Senator Bernie Sanders have prioritized climate change as an essential issue requiring attention. Southeast Florida is particularly susceptible to rising sea levels. Four counties in the region established the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact six years ago to coordinate their response and consolidate funding to manage its effects. The issue has received limited focus in the national presidential debates. The mayors presented debate moderators with three questions concerning climate change, all directed toward Rubio. They cautioned that increased sea levels will present a costly challenge to Florida’s economy. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, Florida coastal communities could face a rise in sea level of approximately 2 feet (60 cm) by 2060. SAP had no editorial involvement in its creation or production.

text: Chinese state media tells readers how to survive a nuclear attack. (In this Dec. 6 story, corrects newspaper location to Jilin province, from Jilin city, paragraph one) BEIJING (Reuters) - A state-run newspaper in China’s Jilin province, which borders North Korea and Russia, on Wednesday published a page of advice on how readers can protect themselves from a nuclear weapons attack or explosion. China has expressed concern over North Korea's nuclear and missile program, while also urging the United States and South Korea to refrain from actions that could provoke Pyongyang. U.S. bombers are scheduled to fly over the Korean peninsula on Wednesday as part of large-scale joint military drills with South Korea. North Korea has warned that these drills could bring the Korean Peninsula to the brink of war. The full-page article in the Jilin Daily does not mention potential attacks by North Korea or any other nation, but explains how nuclear weapons differ from conventional arms and instructs individuals on how to protect themselves in the event of an attack. According to the article, nuclear weapons can cause destruction in five ways: light radiation, blast waves, early-stage nuclear radiation, nuclear electromagnetic pulses, and radioactive contamination. The article states that the first four methods can lead to instant fatalities. Individuals who find themselves outdoors during a nuclear attack are advised to lie in a ditch, cover exposed skin with light-colored clothing, or enter a river or lake to reduce the risk of immediate death. The article includes cartoon illustrations depicting methods to remove radioactive contamination, such as washing shoes with water and using cotton buds to clean ears. It also features an image of a child vomiting to illustrate how medical assistance can be sought to expedite the removal of radiation through procedures like stomach pumping and induced urination. The state-backed Global Times, in a commentary on Wednesday, characterized the article as a public service announcement given the circumstances on the Korean peninsula. The commentary noted that if a conflict arises, the Korean peninsula could produce nuclear contaminants, and it is important to consider and discuss countermeasures openly to inform the public. However, the Global Times emphasized that there is no cause for alarm. Last week, North Korea tested what it described as its most advanced intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), which has the capability to reach the entire United States. U.S. President Donald Trump has stated that he would destroy the North Korean regime if it posed a nuclear threat to the United States. China has opposed military intervention and has called for a cessation of the escalating rhetoric between Washington and Pyongyang.

text: Russian credit to cover part of S-400 missile deal with Turkey: agency. MOSCOW (Reuters) - Russia will provide Turkey with partial financing for Ankara's acquisition of S-400 surface-to-air missile systems, as reported by the Interfax news agency on Tuesday, citing a Russian presidential aide. Turkey has been negotiating the purchase of the system for over a year. The move has been viewed by Washington and some NATO allies as a rejection, given the weapons' incompatibility with the alliance's defense systems. Turkish and Russian officials are scheduled to meet next week to finalize the arrangement, according to Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who made the announcement on Monday. Russian President Vladimir Putin stated in Ankara that a credit agreement for the defense industry would be signed with Turkey in the near future. When queried by Interfax regarding whether the Russian financing would encompass the entire cost of the deal, Russian presidential aide Vladimir Kozhin remarked: "Not the whole, partially." He indicated that technical details, including the interest rate, are under discussion and that the Finance Ministry is managing the deal. Turkey anticipates receiving the first missile system in 2019, as noted by Turkish Defence Minister Nurettin Canikli in November. The agreement includes two S-400 systems, with a third optional system.

text: Democrats renew efforts to link banks, Trump and Russia. FRANKFURT/WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Some Democratic members of the U.S. Congress have renewed efforts to explore potential connections between banks such as Germany’s Deutsche Bank (DBKGn.DE), U.S. President Donald Trump, and Russia. Investigations are being conducted in the United States into possible collusion between Trump’s campaign team and Russia during the presidential election campaign in 2016. The White House and the Kremlin have denied any interference in the election. Maxine Waters, ranking Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, informed reporters that she has filed a resolution of inquiry requesting the U.S. Treasury Secretary to provide documents related to President Trump’s financial connections to Russia, certain illegal financial schemes, and other relevant information. The resolution seeks any records of loans or credit from several banks, including Deutsche Bank and Russian lenders Sberbank (SBER.MM) and Gazprombank (GZPRI.MM), to Trump and 22 of his closest associates, including family members and senior White House and campaign advisers. Specifically, the group is pursuing documents that may have been identified by the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network that could indicate any ties between Trump’s finances and Russia. A resolution of inquiry is a legislative tool through which the House can request information from the administration. Waters filed the resolution with the Financial Services Committee, which now has 14 legislative days to address it, either by debating it or voting against it. If the committee, chaired and controlled by Republicans, does not act on the resolution, it may be brought to the floor of the broader House. Waters and four other colleagues have expressed particular interest in obtaining information from Deutsche Bank, which government ethics disclosures identify as one of Trump’s largest lenders. Deutsche Bank’s lawyers have declined requests for information, citing privacy laws. Waters inquired with Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen at a hearing on Wednesday whether the U.S. central bank had found any information about Trump in its regulatory work regarding Deutsche Bank. Yellen stated that the Fed had not investigated the matter.

text: Peru's Kuczynski urges people to accept Fujimori pardon and 'turn the page'. LIMA (Reuters) - Peru's President Pedro Pablo Kuczynski defended his pardon for Alberto Fujimori on Monday, describing it as justified clemency for an ailing individual whose authoritarian government in the 1990s contributed to the country’s progress, following protests from Peruvians for a second consecutive day. In his first address to the nation since pardoning Fujimori on Christmas Eve, Kuczynski appealed to the public to 'turn the page' and accept the decision. This pardon has placed Kuczynski's center-right administration in a new political crisis, occurring shortly after Congress nearly removed him from office due to a graft scandal. Earlier on Monday, police deployed tear gas to disperse crowds in downtown Lima amid ongoing unrest, while a third lawmaker announced his departure from Kuczynski's political party. Fujimori, who is also 79 years old, remains a polarizing figure in Peru. While many regard him as a corrupt dictator, others acknowledge his role in resolving a severe economic crisis and suppressing a leftist insurgency during his decade in power. The pardon absolved Fujimori of convictions related to graft and human rights violations, 12 years into a 25-year prison sentence. Kuczynski, a former Wall Street banker, reiterated that the pardon was motivated by concerns regarding Fujimori's health. However, for the first time since his election a year ago, he also defended Fujimori's time in office, stating, 'It’s clear his government, which inherited a country submerged in a violent and chaotic crisis at the start of the 1990s, incurred significant legal transgressions regarding democracy and human rights. But I also think his government contributed to national progress,' Kuczynski noted during a televised address. These comments have positioned Kuczynski more closely with Fujimori, inviting renewed criticism from opponents of Fujimori. Gisela Ortiz, a Peruvian human rights activist, remarked on Twitter following Kuczynski's speech, 'You’ve got to be pretty stingy, President Kuczynski, to not say a word of solidarity for the victims and their loved ones.' Just one week prior, Kuczynski expressed concerns over a potential resurgence of Fujimori’s right-wing movement, labeling its legislative efforts to remove him as a coup attempt that jeopardized Peru’s democracy. Many of Fujimori’s critics, who supported Kuczynski in last year’s runoff election, called on lawmakers to reject the presidential vacancy motion. However, a faction among Fujimori's supporters in Congress unexpectedly aided Kuczynski, which has led to speculation about a possible agreement involving votes in exchange for Fujimori's pardon. Leftist lawmaker Marisa Glave stated on local TV channel Canal N, 'The pardon’s for President Kuczynski, it’s not for Fujimori.' Alberto Borea, the lawyer who represented Kuczynski before Congress last week, expressed opposition to the pardon, stating he was unaware of it being planned. Many Peruvians, chanting 'traitor' and 'the pardon has got to go,' participated in marches on Monday, demanding Kuczynski's resignation and new elections. To date, three lawmakers from the ruling party have announced their resignations, which holds approximately one-fifth of congressional seats. A source within the government confirmed the resignation of the deputy human rights minister. Fujimori remains in a hospital in Lima, where he was transferred from prison late on Sunday to address a decline in his blood pressure and an irregular heartbeat, as reported by his doctor.

text: U.N. seeks 'massive' help for Rohingya fleeing Myanmar 'ethnic cleansing'. DHAKA/YANGON (Reuters) - The United Nations on Thursday called for substantial assistance for nearly 400,000 Muslims from Myanmar who have sought refuge in Bangladesh, amid increasing concerns that the number could continue to rise unless Myanmar addresses what critics describe as ethnic cleansing. The Rohingya are leaving due to a military offensive by Myanmar in the western state of Rakhine, which commenced following a series of guerrilla attacks on Aug. 25 targeting security posts and an army camp, resulting in approximately a dozen fatalities. "We urge the international community to enhance humanitarian support and develop solutions," said Mohammed Abdiker, director of operations and emergencies for the International Organisation for Migration, during a news conference in the Bangladeshi capital. He emphasized that the need was considerable. The ongoing violence in Rakhine and the exodus of refugees represent significant challenges for Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who has faced this issue since assuming national leadership last year. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, along with the U.N. Security Council on Wednesday, called on Myanmar to cease the violence, which he characterized as ethnic cleansing. The government of predominantly Buddhist Myanmar disputes these claims, asserting that its actions are aimed at combating terrorism. Numerous Rohingya villages in northern Rakhine have been destroyed, though authorities deny that security forces or Buddhist civilians were responsible for the fires, attributing them instead to the insurgents, and stating that 30,000 non-Muslim villagers were also displaced. Reports from a Reuters journalist in Bangladesh indicate that smoke was observed rising from at least five locations on the Myanmar side of the border on Thursday, although it remains unclear what was ablaze or who initiated the fires. While ethnic cleansing is not recognized as an independent crime under international law, the U.N. Office on Genocide Prevention notes that it has been referenced in U.N. resolutions and acknowledged in decisions by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. text: Trump foreign policies could impact his business interests. LONDON (Reuters) - Any moves by Donald Trump to ban Muslims from entering the United States or reinstate waterboarding for interrogating suspects may have implications for some of his foreign business interests — including his golf course in Scotland and luxury resorts in Indonesia. A review of press releases from the Trump Organization indicates that 15 of 25 new acquisitions or joint ventures announced over the past five years were located overseas. These acquisitions include golf courses in Ireland and Scotland as well as licensing agreements with developers and manufacturers in Dubai, Indonesia, India, Azerbaijan, Brazil, Mexico, and Panama. The transactions highlight potential conflicts of interest Trump may encounter after he assumes the presidency on January 20, as well as his susceptibility to accusations of being influenced by foreign entities. Foreign governments might attempt to leverage Trump’s business interests to influence his decision-making or to impose financial consequences for actions they disapprove of. Trump’s transition team opted not to comment on this story. In the 16 months leading up to May, Trump reportedly earned up to $23 million from licensing his name to developers in emerging markets, according to a filing with the U.S. Office of Government Ethics. "The licensing deals are the best of all because there’s no risk," Trump stated in a June interview with Reuters. "I have 121 deals right now, going forward, right now, 121, all over the world, in China, in Indonesia," he added. However, his meeting with Indian business partners last week drew criticism regarding the perceived lack of separation between Trump and his business. The Trump Organization has stated that a business structure will be established to comply with "all applicable rules and regulations." Trump has not yet committed to creating a blind trust that would formally disconnect him from his business interests. "I’m very confident he’s not breaking any laws," Kellyanne Conway, a senior adviser to Trump, informed reporters at Trump Tower in New York on Monday. Analysts suggest Trump could face backlash against his business interests in Middle Eastern and Asian markets if he implements his campaign promise to ban Muslims from entering the United States and continues to consider reinstating waterboarding or establishing a national registry for Muslims. "If the Muslim registry is introduced, he will have serious issues finding Muslim local partners," remarked Professor Koen Pauwels, a marketing expert at Ozyegin University in Istanbul. Last year, his daughter Ivanka mentioned that the organization was in discussions regarding deals in Qatar and Saudi Arabia. Trump has a licensing agreement with a developer for a Trump-branded retail complex in Istanbul. He has also secured agreements in Indonesia, the world’s most populous Muslim nation, to brand a redeveloped luxury golf resort in Java and a luxury hotel and residential development in Bali. text: Myanmar, accused of crackdown, invited to U.S.-Thai military exercise. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Myanmar military, which has faced allegations of ethnic cleansing against the country’s Muslim Rohingya minority, has received an invitation to return as an observer in a significant multinational military exercise scheduled for next year, led by the United States and Thailand. Lieutenant Colonel Christopher Logan, a Pentagon spokesman, informed Reuters that Thailand had invited Myanmar to participate in the annual Cobra Gold exercise, which involves thousands of U.S. and Thai military personnel along with participants from other Asian countries. According to Logan, Myanmar has been invited to observe the humanitarian assistance and disaster relief segment of the exercise. A senior officer at the Directorate of Joint Intelligence of the Royal Thai Armed Forces stated to Reuters that it was uncertain whether Myanmar had accepted the invitation, but Thailand expressed a desire for their participation. When asked about the rationale behind Thailand's invitation to Myanmar, given the ongoing concerns regarding the crackdown on the Rohingya, the official remarked: 'That never came up in the discussions. We separated that issue (the Rohingya). We focus on training, on education, on military cooperation. That is our wish, to have Myanmar involved. That is politics. We are soldiers. This is a military exercise.' The official chose to remain unnamed as they were not authorized to address the media. The Myanmar military did not respond to multiple requests for comment. When inquired whether the U.S. military had sought to apply pressure on Thailand not to extend the invitation to Myanmar due to international condemnation of its actions, the Pentagon refrained from commenting on internal deliberations. The Myanmar military conducted a crackdown on the Muslim Rohingya from Rakhine state following attacks by Rohingya militants on an army base and police posts in August. This crackdown has resulted in approximately 650,000 Rohingya fleeing to Bangladesh in recent months. Both the United States and the United Nations have characterized the campaign as ethnic cleansing of the stateless Rohingya people. The Myanmar military has stated that its internal investigation found security forces exonerated of all accusations of atrocities in Rakhine. However, earlier this week, the United States imposed sanctions on 13 individuals identified as serious human rights abusers and corrupt actors, including Myanmar general Maung Maung Soe, who oversaw the crackdown against the Rohingya. Zachary Abuza, a professor at the U.S. National War College, commented that inviting Myanmar to the exercise was 'outrageous' and conveyed an inappropriate message. He stated, 'To invite them after what the U.S. government has labeled ethnic cleansing, when the Treasury Department just yesterday designated the commander for these egregious violations of human rights, just seems wrong, and that is putting it too mildly.' Abuza specializes in Southeast Asia and security issues, including human rights. In the 2017 Cobra Gold exercise, 29 nations either participated or observed, including Myanmar, and it involved approximately 3,600 U.S. personnel. Cobra Gold is an annual exercise conducted in Thailand, with the 2018 war games anticipated to occur in February. The United States and Thailand have engaged in joint military exercises for decades, despite Bangkok’s human rights and democracy record often facing criticism in Washington. The U.S.-Thai relationship experienced a downturn following the Thai military's acquisition of power in a 2014 coup but has seen improvements under President Donald Trump. Reporters Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo have been detained for nine days without information on their location and have not had access to visitors or legal counsel.

text: Senate Republicans tie tax plan to repeal of key Obamacare mandate. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - On Tuesday, U.S. Senate Republicans linked the repeal of a key component of Obamacare to their tax-cut plan, introducing new political risks and uncertainties for the tax measure that financial markets have been monitoring closely for months. Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell stated to reporters: "We’re optimistic that inserting the individual mandate repeal would be helpful and that’s obviously the view of the Senate Finance Committee Republicans as well." The finance panel, which had been in session for two days, adjourned on Tuesday as Democrats criticized the Republicans’ handling of the tax proposals, for which formal legislative language has not yet been unveiled. Ron Wyden, the committee’s top Democrat, requested additional time for Democrats to discuss the issue, stating, "because we were never told that healthcare was going to be part of it and this just flew in literally out of nowhere in the last 20 minutes." Connecting Obamacare to the tax program introduces new challenges for the Republicans and for President Donald Trump. They have not yet achieved a significant legislative win since Trump assumed office in January, despite having control of Congress and the White House. Trump suggested in a tweet on Monday that the mandate repeal should be included in the tax plan, a follow-up to a similar tweet on Nov. 3. No final decision regarding this matter was made at the Senate Republicans’ weekly luncheon, according to Senator Susan Collins. She had a significant role in July’s failure to repeal Obamacare, formally known as the Affordable Care Act. "I personally think that it complicates tax reform to put the repeal of the individual mandate in there," Collins remarked. When asked if she would support the tax bill if a mandate repeal were included, she stated, "I’m going to wait and see." Senator John McCain, who was also involved in the party’s unsuccessful Obamacare repeal earlier this year, expressed uncertainty regarding the inclusion of the mandate repeal in the tax plan, saying, "I want to see the whole bill before I decide." The Senate and House of Representatives are developing separate tax-cut packages that they plan to reconcile and send to Trump’s desk for enactment into law, an outcome Republicans are aiming to achieve to present at least one major legislative achievement to U.S. voters next year. House Speaker Paul Ryan, when asked why the repeal of the Obamacare mandate was not included in the House version of the tax proposal, stated to Fox News on Tuesday, "We didn’t want to complicate tax reform, make it harder than it otherwise would be." He noted that the House had already agreed to eliminate the mandate in a healthcare bill passed in May, adding, "We want to see the Senate go first and see if they can get that done and then we’ll discuss whether or not it’s included at the end." The Trump administration strongly supports the House version of the tax legislation, stating that its passage would be "an important first step in achieving comprehensive tax reform," according to the White House in a statement on Tuesday. U.S. financial markets have been closely monitoring the situation, with U.S. stocks rallying in recent months, partly due to expectations of business tax cuts. They showed little reaction to Tuesday’s developments. The individual mandate requires Americans to have health insurance or pay a penalty, a provision that Republicans have opposed as government overreach. However, the mandate plays a critical role in Obamacare by requiring young, healthy individuals, who might otherwise go without coverage, to purchase insurance and help offset the costs of covering sicker and older Americans.

TOKYO (Reuters) - Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe plans to highlight the significance of the Japan-U.S. alliance during his meeting with President-elect Donald Trump on Thursday, according to Foreign Minister Fumio Kishida, who spoke on Sunday. "This is going to be an important meeting to build trust," Kishida told public broadcaster NHK. "We also would like to use this opportunity to input the importance of the Japan-U.S. alliance, as well." Abe is scheduled to meet Trump in New York before attending an Asia-Pacific summit in Peru. Tokyo is seeking clarity on the direction that the Republican political novice intends for bilateral relations, following comments made during the campaign that diverged from established policies. Kishida reiterated Japan’s longstanding position that it has no plans to possess nuclear weapons. During his campaign, Trump left open the possibility that Japan - the only country to have suffered a nuclear bombing - might adopt nuclear weapons. "I don’t believe Japan will possess nuclear arms. This principle won’t change," Kishida stated. Trump's campaign remarks regarding Japan’s potential nuclear armament and his request that Japan contribute more financially for the upkeep of U.S. forces stationed in Japan have raised concerns in Tokyo about a potential rift in the security alliance with Washington, which has been fundamental to Japan's defense since World War Two. Defence Minister Tomomi Inada commented on the same NHK program that Japan is already bearing a significant financial burden to support U.S. troops stationed in Japan. "Japan is making sufficient contribution," she said. "I would like to continue underscoring that Japan is going to strengthen its own defense posture both in quality and quantity, strengthen the Japan-U.S. alliance and strengthen ties with other relevant countries."

text: Senator McCain wants hearing on possible F-16 sale to Pakistan. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Senator John McCain on Thursday urged the Senate Foreign Relations Committee to hold a hearing on the possible sale of Lockheed Martin Corp F-16 fighter jets to Pakistan, as more lawmakers expressed concern about the deal. McCain, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, told reporters he was concerned about the timing of the Obama administration’s decision to approve the sale of the fighter jets to Pakistan, and the potential consequences for U.S. relations with India. “I would rather have seen it kicked over into the next administration,” McCain said. A hearing would help senators decide what to do about the proposed sale, he said, noting he was very “conflicted.” The U.S. government announced on Feb. 12 that it had approved the sale to Pakistan of up to eight additional F-16 fighter jets, as well as radars and other equipment in a deal valued at $699 million. The deal drew immediate criticism from India. Separately, U.S. Senator Rand Paul said Thursday he had introduced a resolution of disapproval seeking to halt U.S. arms sales to Pakistan’s government. If passed, the measure would stop the F-16 sale. U.S. lawmakers have until March 12 to block the sale. Such action is rare since deals are usually well vetted before any formal notification, and it remained unclear if lawmakers would thwart the deal. State Department spokesman David McKeeby said the proposed sale of F-16s would assist Pakistan’s counterterrorism and counterinsurgency operations and was in the interests of Pakistan, the United States, NATO and the region. “Pakistan’s current F-16s have proven critical to the success of these operations to date. These operations reduce the ability of militants to use Pakistani territory as a safe haven for terrorism and a base of support for the insurgency in Afghanistan,” he said. McKeeby said the department was aware of congressional concerns and would continue to consult and engage with lawmakers. Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Bob Corker allowed the Obama administration to proceed with the deal, but said he would not approve using U.S. funds to pay for the planes through the foreign military financing (FMF) program. Corker told Secretary of State John Kerry in a letter earlier this month that he was concerned about Pakistan’s ties to the Haqqani network, a militant group that U.S. officials have said is behind attacks in Afghanistan.

text: Michigan state House approves carrying concealed guns without permit. (Reuters) - Legislation to allow Michigan gun owners to carry a concealed handgun without a permit was approved in the state House of Representatives on Wednesday, following similar actions in a dozen other states. The package of four bills cleared the Republican-controlled House with some support from Democrats and now moves to the Senate, which is also under Republican control. It is currently unclear if Michigan’s Republican Governor Rick Snyder supports the bill. If the Senate also approves the measure, it could become law automatically 14 days after reaching the governor’s desk unless he vetoes it. The legislation would eliminate the requirement for handgun owners to obtain a concealed pistol license, which comes with a $100 fee, to carry the weapon in public. Handgun owners would also be permitted to carry a concealed pistol in public without the required firearms training. Proponents of the bill argue it supports the U.S. constitutional right to bear arms. “We all know criminals are not paying fees, taking classes and waiting for approval to come in the mail before they begin carrying guns,” said Michigan state Representative Michele Hoitenga, who sponsored the bill. She indicated that the legislation “levels the playing field for honest people.” Critics of the bill have described it as potentially hazardous. Twelve other U.S. states currently allow gun owners to carry their weapons without a concealed-carry permit, as reported by the Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence. Most of these states are conservative-leaning with Republican-majority legislatures, although Vermont, which has a Democratic-controlled statehouse, is included among them. “The states that have eliminated the permit requirement are basically making it easier to carry a gun in public than drive a car,” stated Hannah Shearer, a staff attorney with the San Francisco-based Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence. Legislation introduced in the U.S. Congress this year would, if passed and signed by President Donald Trump, mandate all states to permit firearm owners to carry their guns under the regulations of their home state, even when visiting other states. For instance, a person allowed to carry a concealed firearm without a permit in North Dakota could do so while visiting California or New York state, where permits are required, Shearer noted.

text: Chinese general kills himself amid corruption probe. BEIJING (Reuters) - A Chinese general under investigation for corruption has reportedly committed suicide, according to state media on Tuesday. This incident is part of a broader anti-graft campaign affecting the armed forces. Zhang Yang, a former member of the Central Military Commission (CMC), was being investigated for his connections to former generals Guo Boxiong and Xu Caihou, as reported by the official Xinhua news agency. text: Bangladesh has approved a $280 million project to develop an isolated and flood-prone island in the Bay of Bengal for the temporary housing of 100,000 Rohingya Muslims fleeing violence in Myanmar. The decision was made shortly after Bangladesh finalized a deal to begin the repatriation of Rohingya to Myanmar within two months, aiming to alleviate pressure on existing refugee camps. A committee led by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina endorsed the plan to develop Bhashan Char island, also known as Thenger Char, despite concerns raised by humanitarian organizations regarding the island's habitability. Planning Minister Mustafa Kamal stated that while repatriation will take time, Bangladesh requires a location to accommodate the refugees in the interim. The project is expected to be completed by 2019. Many Rohingya individuals are currently facing severe living conditions, and Kamal characterized the influx of refugees as a potential risk to security and the environment. Over 620,000 Rohingya Muslims have sought refuge in Bangladesh following a military counter-insurgency operation in Myanmar's Rakhine State, which was initiated after attacks by Rohingya militants on military and police facilities on August 25. In September, Bangladesh Foreign Minister Abul Hassan Mahmood Ali called for international assistance in transporting Rohingya to the island. Prior to the recent influx, approximately 300,000 Rohingya refugees were already present in Bangladesh. The country, one of the most densely populated and economically challenged in the world, plans to develop the island that emerged from silt off the delta coast of Bangladesh just 11 years ago, located two hours by boat from the nearest settlement. The island is prone to flooding during the monsoon season from June to September, and nearby waters are known to be patrolled by pirates who target fishermen for ransom. The proposal to develop the island for refugee accommodation was initially put forward in 2015 and was revisited last year. Despite ongoing criticism regarding the island's conditions, Bangladesh maintains that it has the authority to determine the location for housing the increasing number of refugees.

text: Palestinians may seek U.N. Assembly support if U.S. vetoes Jerusalem resolution: envoy. DUBAI (Reuters) - The Palestinian leadership may turn to the U.N. General Assembly if Washington vetoes a draft U.N. Security Council resolution to reaffirm Jerusalem's status as unresolved, following President Donald Trump’s decision to recognize it as Israel’s capital. The Palestinian United Nations envoy raised this option in remarks published in Saudi daily Arab News on Monday, ahead of a Security Council vote on an Egyptian-drafted resolution regarding Jerusalem's status, which the United States is expected to veto. The draft states that any decisions and actions which purport to have altered the character, status or demographic composition of the Holy City of Jerusalem have no legal effect, are null and void and must be rescinded. Trump’s Dec. 6 decision to recognize Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and to move the U.S. Embassy to the city has prompted widespread anger and protests among Palestinians, as well as broad international criticism, including from key U.S. allies. Israel contends that Jerusalem is its indivisible capital. It captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it, a move that has not received international recognition. Palestinians seek East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state in territory captured by Israel fifty years ago. Arab News quoted Ambassador Riyad Mansour as stating that the Palestinians and Egyptians have collaborated closely with Security Council members while drafting the resolution to ensure it receives substantial support. The Europeans, in particular, requested the avoidance of terms such as 'denounce' and 'condemn' and requested that the U.S. not be mentioned by name, according to Mansour. He noted that they complied with these requests but maintained the active clauses rejecting all changes to Jerusalem and reaffirming previous decisions. Israel has long alleged that the United Nations is biased against it in its conflict with the Palestinians, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reiterated support for Trump’s decision on Sunday. The Palestinians have the option of invoking a rarely-used article of the U.N. Charter that calls for disputing parties not to exercise a veto, Arab News reported. However, it noted that they are more likely to bring the issue to the General Assembly under Resolution 377A, known as the 'Uniting for Peace' resolution. Resolution 377A was adopted in 1950 and was used to authorize the deployment of U.S. troops in the Korean War. Mansour indicated that Palestinians utilized the 'Uniting for Peace' resolution in the 1990s after Israel commenced construction on a settlement at Jabal Abut Ghnaim, a hilltop on occupied West Bank land south of Jerusalem, but left that session in suspension. However, he stated they could seek to resume the session. If the resolution is vetoed, the Palestinian delegation can send a letter to the U.N. Secretary General requesting the resumption of the emergency session, he explained, according to Arab News.

text: Senator Warren criticizes Equifax potential to profit from breach. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized Equifax Inc (EFX.N) on Wednesday, stating that the company failed to adequately protect customers following a significant data breach that compromised information belonging to more than 140 million individuals. "The breach of your system has actually created more business opportunities for you," Warren, a Democrat recognized for her consumer advocacy, remarked to former Equifax Chief Executive Officer Richard Smith during his second congressional testimony this week. In addition to offering consumer credit reports, Equifax provides products designed to protect individuals' data from misuse. Warren indicated that this business combination results in a conflict of interest, as Equifax is responsible for safeguarding consumer data while simultaneously profiting from consumers' efforts to address the breach. "Equifax is making money, millions of dollars off its own screw-up and meanwhile the potential cost to Equifax are shockingly low," Warren stated to Smith, 57, during the U.S. Senate Banking Committee hearing. Smith, who retired from the credit reporting company last week, led the firm during the period of the breach, which was disclosed last month. Smith acknowledged that the hack posed a risk for fraud and that the company could benefit from consumers seeking to secure their data. However, he defended Equifax’s overall social utility. The company collects data on consumers which it sells to banks to assist in evaluating a borrower's creditworthiness. "The company has been around for 118 years and for most of those 118 years has done good things," Smith said. After the hearing, Warren informed reporters that Equifax’s new product allowing individuals to "lock" and "unlock" their credit reports does not offer adequate protection, asserting that only legislative changes can fully safeguard individuals' information. "It only applies to Equifax. Consumers are now vulnerable to the loss of their data and some thief going through one of the other credit reporting agencies. That’s why we need to change the law. We need to make it in place forever and make sure consumers have control over their own data," she stated. Wednesday’s hearing was the second of four hearings for Smith this week as lawmakers continue to review the breach. Several lawmakers on Wednesday also raised questions regarding why Equifax was awarded a contract with the Internal Revenue Service to assist in verifying taxpayer data. Speaking before Congress on Tuesday, Smith repeatedly expressed regret for the breach, indicating that it took weeks for the credit bureau to fully comprehend the scope of the intrusion.

text: U.S. House Republicans finalize list of rules to eliminate in Wednesday vote. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Republicans continued their deregulatory efforts on Tuesday, as the U.S. House of Representatives Rules Committee officially included a regulation on methane and one aimed at addressing pay discrimination to the list of rules to be voted on for repeal on Wednesday. On Monday, the committee also forwarded three other recently enacted rules concerning the environment, corruption, and firearms to the full House for elimination under the Congressional Review Act, which has seen effective usage only once since its inception in 2001. The Republican-controlled House is anticipated to vote on Wednesday to rescind all five regulations before passing them to the Senate. Agencies are prohibited from instituting a new rule to replace any part of a regulation that has been overturned, and Democrats during Tuesday’s committee hearing contended that House Republicans were limiting the potential for future regulatory measures that might be necessary. They also requested additional time to evaluate the rollback of regulations that typically require extensive time to develop. Representative Jim McGovern, a Democrat from Massachusetts, stated, “What we’ve been doing today and yesterday ... I would characterize as mindless legislating.” He expressed concern that this process may expose numerous vulnerable individuals and working populations, as well as the environment, to unfavorable consequences. Louise Slaughter, the committee’s senior Democrat from New York, expressed her disagreement with the methane rule during the one-hour hearing, stating, “I disagree wholeheartedly with what you’re doing.” However, Democrats possess limited capacity to prevent the revocation of regulations, as only simple majorities in both chambers are required for a rule’s repeal. Previously, attempts by Republicans to nullify regulations faced veto threats from former president Barack Obama, a Democrat. Currently, President Donald Trump, a Republican, occupies the White House. Critics of the methane rule argue that it is unnecessary, claiming it is a redundant regulation that infringes on state rights and complicates the distribution of natural gas due to excessive bureaucratic procedures. Supporters, on the other hand, contend that the rule prevents oil and gas companies from polluting the environment, generates royalties for the federal government, and minimizes methane waste. Those advocating for the repeal of the pay-discrimination rule express similar concerns, arguing that existing regulations already address this issue and that the requirement for federal contractors to gather employee information will incur significant costs and time.

text: U.S. Air Force awards contracts to Raytheon, Lockheed for next-generation cruise missile. (Reuters) - The U.S. Air Force has awarded Lockheed Martin Corp and Raytheon Co separate contracts worth $900 million each to advance the development of a replacement for the AGM-86B air-launched nuclear cruise missile, as announced by the Pentagon on Wednesday. The award for the new Long Range Standoff weapon (LRSO) coincides with increasing tensions with North Korea; however, the Air Force had solicited proposals from the defense industry last summer to replace the aging nuclear cruise missiles and intercontinental ballistic missile system as part of a broader modernization effort of its aging atomic weapons systems. “This weapon will modernize the air-based leg of the nuclear triad,” said Secretary of the Air Force Heather Wilson in a statement. According to Lockheed Martin, the LRSO, which is a plane-launched weapon, “will be capable of penetrating and surviving advanced integrated air defense systems from significant standoff range.” The contract awards facilitate parallel detailed development and prototyping for the cruise missile replacement over the next four and a half years, focusing on technology maturation and risk reduction of the weapon. Following this phase, the Air Force will select a single contractor for engineering, manufacturing, and deployment. The Air Force aims to procure approximately 1,000 LRSO flight bodies, with the development and procurement costs projected to be around $10 billion, as stated by an Air Force spokesperson. Some of the flight bodies will be equipped with nuclear weapons, while others will serve for testing or as spares. The Air Force has indicated plans to begin fielding the LRSO by 2030. The current cruise missile was first introduced in the early 1980s and has a lifespan of 10 years. On Monday, the Air Force also awarded Boeing Co and Northrop Grumman Corp separate contracts to continue work on replacing the aging Minuteman III ICBM system. The modernization of the U.S. nuclear force is anticipated to exceed $350 billion over the next decade. The United States is set to replace its aging systems, which include bombs, nuclear bombers, missiles, and submarines. Some analysts have estimated the total cost at $1 trillion over 30 years.

text: U.S. Senate confirms Trump's pick for top Supreme Court lawyer. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Republican-controlled U.S. Senate on Tuesday confirmed President Donald Trump’s nominee to serve as his administration’s top advocate before the U.S. Supreme Court, overcoming united Democratic opposition. Noel Francisco, a Washington lawyer with strong conservative credentials who previously worked in Republican former President George W. Bush’s administration, was confirmed by the Senate as U.S. solicitor general on a vote of 50-47. All the Senate’s Democrats voted against him except for New Jersey’s Robert Menendez, who is currently on trial facing corruption charges in Newark. Francisco takes up his new position as the Supreme Court prepares to begin its new term on Oct. 2. The court has several potential blockbuster cases on its docket, including the challenge to Trump’s travel ban on people from six predominantly Muslim countries entering the United States. That case will be argued before the justices on Oct. 10. Francisco, who previously worked at the Jones Day law firm, will now be overseeing the Justice Department’s defense of the ban and other major policy initiatives that are challenged in court. He has argued three cases at the Supreme Court. Most recently, he represented Republican former Virginia Governor Robert McDonnell in a successful attempt to throw out corruption convictions. The justices ruled in favor of McDonnell last year in an 8-0 ruling that could make it tougher to prosecute politicians for corruption. Francisco served as a White House lawyer from 2001 to 2003 and spent another two years in the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel from 2003 to 2005. He previously worked as a clerk for the late Supreme Court conservative Justice Antonin Scalia.

text: Czech election front-runner likely to influence state-owned CEZ. PRAGUE (Reuters) - Andrej Babis has indicated that he intends to manage the Czech Republic with a business-oriented approach, which may lead to changes for the country's largest state-controlled enterprise, CEZ. The billionaire Babis has previously clashed with CEZ management, and with his ANO party polling ahead of the parliamentary elections scheduled for Friday and Saturday, he may soon gain the authority to address the management he believes has mismanaged the company. "The fact that CEZ is out of his control and he doesn’t have a say in it has troubled him considerably," said Jiri Pehe, a political analyst and director at New York University in Prague. As one of the leading business figures in the country, he seeks to have CEZ under his influence. CEZ is 70 percent state-owned, boasting a market capitalization of $11.3 billion, making it the largest publicly traded company in the Czech Republic. Historically, it has played a significant role in Czech politics, acting as a substantial revenue source for the government by providing the highest dividends among state-controlled firms. Its investment initiatives generate considerable business for various Czech suppliers. Daniel Benes has been the chief executive since 2011, having joined the board six years prior. His contract extends for another four years and he has received support from previous prime ministers, including the outgoing Social Democrat Bohuslav Sobotka. This support may cease if Babis assumes office following Saturday’s elections. Babis, whose business portfolio includes food, chemical, and media sectors, has consistently argued that CEZ exerts excessive influence over political parties, a concern he reiterated in a recent interview. "In my view, one state firm cannot run all political parties and cannot be a piggy bank for politicians," Babis stated in the magazine Tyden. A spokesperson for CEZ declined to comment on his statements. During his tenure as finance minister from January 2014 to May of this year, Babis had confrontations with CEZ management but lacked sufficient authority to implement significant changes. As prime minister, he would gain more influence and could alter the supervisory board that appoints management. Over the past year, Babis has expressed disapproval of a dividend reduction, a potential sale of a coal plant, and a proposal currently under review to spin off regulated distribution and renewable assets. This proposed spin-off would separate and possibly sell CEZ's distribution and renewable segments while allowing the government to maintain full control over its nuclear and coal facilities. This would enable the government to undertake the construction of new nuclear plants. Conversely, Babis contends that CEZ should fund the construction of nuclear plants independently. CEZ management has indicated it would not proceed without explicit state guarantees to support financing. Miroslav Frayer, who monitors the utility for Komercni Banka, remarked that the proposed spin-off is an issue the government will need to address promptly. Michal Snobr, a seasoned CEZ investor representing a group with nearly 1 percent ownership in the company, anticipates changes following the election. "Given how Babis is presenting it, there are likely to be changes in the CEZ leadership," Snobr remarked. He noted that this management has committed numerous errors that would typically prompt changes in a standard business context. He highlighted prolonged outages at CEZ's nuclear facility in Dukovany, a lack of strategic direction, and current projects such as acquisitions of expensive German wind plants. Snobr suggested that a spin-off of CEZ could proceed similarly to the separation of Innogy from RWE in Germany, especially given the high valuations of regulated businesses. He added that Babis may revise his stance after the election. Additionally, Snobr indicated that CEZ would not be able to finance new nuclear plants without state support, as such a significant investment would not be commercially viable and could result in legal challenges from other shareholders.

text: NRA gun rights group pours money into Republican U.S. Senate campaigns. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The National Rifle Association is expected to achieve record spending this year on U.S. political campaigns, including Missouri’s U.S. Senate race where a gun-owning Democrat is competing against an incumbent Republican who is supported by the gun rights group. Democrat Jason Kander, an Afghanistan war veteran, is trailing Republican U.S. Senator Roy Blunt by 2.5 percentage points in opinion polls in Missouri, despite the NRA’s expenditure of $1.8 million to support Blunt and the Republicans’ U.S. Senate majority. Gun violence has drawn significant attention in the United States in 2016, highlighted by incidents such as a massacre at an Orlando, Florida, nightclub and a series of police shootings, prompting some Democrats and activists to call for stricter gun laws. These initiatives have faced challenges, as in previous years, from the NRA and its supporters, who argue that such measures would violate the right to bear arms as established by the Second Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. Since the 1990s, Congress has not passed major gun-control legislation. An Aug. 19 Reuters/Ipsos poll indicated that 41.8 percent of respondents supported strong restrictions on firearms, while 22.4 percent favored moderate regulations. Per-capita firearm ownership in the United States significantly exceeds that of any other country, according to government estimates. In the Missouri race and other Senate contests in states such as North Carolina, Nevada, Florida, and New Hampshire, the gun-control debate is being addressed on the campaign trail. The NRA has spent $23.4 million in this election cycle, with one month remaining before the elections on Nov. 8, compared to a previous high of $27 million in the entire 2014 campaign cycle, according to federal data from the Center for Responsive Politics. The NRA did not respond to requests for comment. In addition to Senate Republicans, the lobbying group is also supporting Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump. Blunt, 66, has served in Congress for two decades. He accuses Kander, 35, of being lenient on gun ownership rights. Blunt holds an “A” rating from the NRA, while Kander has received an “F,” which the NRA attributes to Kander’s support for expanded background checks on gun buyers and legislation introduced this year in Congress aimed at preventing individuals on “terrorism watch lists” from purchasing firearms. Kander stated, “The difference between Senator Blunt and myself is that I want to stop criminals and suspected terrorists from having the same access to guns as the rest of us, which is why I support background checks.” Kander, Missouri’s secretary of state, released a 30-second TV commercial last month that has garnered over 1 million views on youtube.com. In the advertisement, the former U.S. Army captain assembles a military-style rifle while blindfolded. He asserts his support for gun ownership rights but adds, “I also believe in background checks so that terrorists can’t get their hands on one of these.” A significant debate in Washington concerning background checks in June resulted in a 25-hour sit-in by Democrats on the floor of the House of Representatives. Tim Daly, managing director of guns and crime policy for the liberal Center For American Progress, stated, “The reaction to that ad has reset the debate” in the Missouri Senate race. Kander’s polling numbers were already improving when the ad was first aired on Sept. 15. However, Daly noted that Kander raised new questions regarding the NRA's stance on background checks. Blunt and his campaign representatives were not available for comment. The NRA is Blunt’s second-largest financial supporter in the Missouri race, following a group closely aligned with U.S. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell that backs Republicans. Similar to the Blunt-Kander contest, other significant 2016 Senate races demonstrate an ongoing debate over gun issues as Republicans strive to maintain their control of the Senate.

Democrat Jason Kander, an Afghanistan war veteran, is running just 2.5 percentage points behind Republican U.S. Senator Roy Blunt in opinion polls in Missouri, despite the NRA’s expenditure of $1.8 million so far trying to protect Blunt as well as the Republicans’ U.S. Senate majority. Gun violence has transfixed the United States in 2016, from a massacre at an Orlando, Florida, nightclub to a rash of police shootings, fueling demands by some Democrats and activists for tighter gun laws. Those efforts have been thwarted, as in years past, by the NRA and its supporters, who say such measures would infringe on the right to bear arms guaranteed

text: Sea surges may impact parts of Florida: Governor Scott. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - A significant sea surge is expected to accompany Hurricane Irma as the storm progresses through Florida, and this influx of ocean water may cause considerable damage to coastal areas, according to Florida Governor Rick Scott. He expressed particular concern about the west coast, referring to Florida's western shoreline that faces the Gulf of Mexico and is experiencing severe effects from Irma. Scott made these statements during an appearance on Fox News Sunday. Later, on ABC News, he remarked: This storm surge is just deadly.

text: Iran urges Muslim nations to defend Palestinians after Trump move. ISTANBUL (Reuters) - Iranian President Hassan Rouhani stated on Wednesday that all Muslim nations should collaborate to defend the rights of Palestinians following Donald Trump's decision last week to recognize Jerusalem as Israel's capital. Rouhani, who was attending an emergency meeting of Muslim leaders, indicated that the U.S. president's decision demonstrated a lack of respect for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people. Iran is prepared to work with all Muslim countries without any preconditions to defend the legitimate rights of Palestinians, Rouhani remarked during the meeting in Istanbul. He emphasized the importance of unity among Muslim nations and stated that Quds (Jerusalem) should be prioritized. Opposition to Israel and support for the Palestinian cause have been fundamental aspects of Iran's foreign policy since the Islamic revolution of 1979 that resulted in the overthrow of the U.S.-backed Shah. Iran, a leading Shiite Muslim power, and Sunni Muslim Saudi Arabia are in competition for influence in the Middle East, where they back opposing groups in Yemen, Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon. Tehran and Riyadh perceive each other as significant threats to regional peace and stability. Saudi Arabia severed diplomatic relations with Iran in 2016 after Iranian protesters attacked Saudi diplomatic missions in Tehran and Mashhad in response to Riyadh's execution of a prominent Shiite cleric. Rouhani advised that Muslim countries should settle their disputes through dialogue and accused Israel of instigating tension across the Middle East. On his Twitter account, Rouhani stated that Trump's recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital indicated that Washington was not a reliable mediator and would not be in the future, adding that it aimed to protect the interests of Zionists. Iran does not recognize Israel and considers Palestine to encompass all of the holy land, including Israeli territory. Iranian leaders have consistently called for the destruction of Israel. Tehran supports several militant Islamist groups in their opposition to Israel.

text: House Democrats support Special Counsel Mueller. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives expressed their support for Special Counsel Robert Mueller on Thursday, following recent efforts by Republicans and conservative news outlets to challenge his credibility and the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. In a letter addressed to Justice Department Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein, 171 of the 193 Democrats in the House indicated their backing for Mueller’s investigation and urged Rosenstein to allow it to proceed without political influence or threats to his authority. California Democrat Maxine Waters stated during a press conference on Thursday, "We will not stand by and allow Fox News and right-wing Republicans to defy the rule of law and create their own rules to interfere with the legitimate investigation under the Constitution of the United States." She further commented, “There is an organized effort by Republicans ... to spin a false narrative and conjure up outrageous scenarios to accuse Special Counsel Mueller of being biased.” Rosenstein appointed Mueller as Special Counsel in May, after President Donald Trump dismissed former FBI Director James Comey, citing the investigation into Russia as a reason. Critics alleged that the president's actions were an attempt to obstruct the investigation. Mueller is examining whether Trump’s presidential campaign colluded with Russia to influence the election. Russia has denied any interference, and Trump has stated that there was no collusion. Republican criticism of Mueller, who is affiliated with their party, has grown in recent months, particularly after he charged four close associates of Trump, including former campaign manager Paul Manafort and former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn. Republicans and hosts on Fox News have claimed that Mueller’s team and the Federal Bureau of Investigation have displayed bias, referencing anti-Trump messages exchanged by two FBI staffers who had previously worked on Mueller’s team. House Republicans have initiated their own investigation into the FBI’s handling of Hillary Clinton’s emails, questioning whether she received preferential treatment after no charges were filed. There have been recent speculations in Washington regarding Trump’s potential intentions to dismiss Mueller, which Trump’s lawyers have denied. Rosenstein, also a Republican, supervises Mueller’s team and stated that he can only terminate Mueller for valid reasons; he informed Congress last week that he sees no legitimate grounds for such an action. House Judiciary Committee Ranking Democrat Jerrold Nadler remarked on Thursday that “this investigation must continue unimpeded,” while suggesting that Republicans were attempting to assist the President as circumstances become more challenging for him.

text: Myanmar's Suu Kyi faces increased pressure as nearly 125,000 Rohingya flee violence. SHAMLAPUR, Bangladesh/DHAKA (Reuters) - Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi is under growing pressure to address violence against Rohingya Muslims, which has resulted in nearly 125,000 individuals fleeing to Bangladesh in just over 10 days. United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned of potential ethnic cleansing and regional destabilization, urging the U.N. Security Council to advocate for restraint and calm in a letter expressing concern about the violence escalating into a humanitarian crisis. Reuters reporters observed hundreds of Rohingya arriving on boats at the Bangladeshi border village of Shamlapur on Tuesday, indicating that the exodus continues. The International Organization for Migration stated that humanitarian assistance needs to be urgently increased, highlighting an immediate funding gap of $18 million over the next three months to enhance lifesaving services for the new arrivals. Indonesian Foreign Minister Retno Marsudi, after discussions with Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in Dhaka, expressed Jakarta's readiness to assist Bangladesh in managing the crisis. She emphasized, "This humanitarian crisis shall be ended," during her remarks to reporters in Dhaka, following talks in the Myanmar capital. The latest outbreak of violence in Myanmar's northwestern Rakhine state began on August 25, when Rohingya insurgents attacked multiple police posts and an army base. The subsequent clashes and military counter-offensive have resulted in at least 400 fatalities and prompted many villagers to flee to Bangladesh. Myanmar officials attribute the destruction of homes and civilian casualties to Rohingya militants, while rights monitors and fleeing Rohingya claim that the Myanmar army is conducting a campaign involving arson and killings to drive them out. When asked if the violence could be characterized as ethnic cleansing, Guterres stated, "We are facing a risk, I hope we don’t get there." He called on all authorities in Myanmar, both civilian and military, to put an end to the violence, which he believes poses a risk of regional destabilization. The treatment of Myanmar's approximately 1.1 million Muslim Rohingya represents a significant challenge for Suu Kyi, who has faced criticism from Western nations for her silence regarding the persecution of this minority group. Myanmar maintains that its security forces are engaged in a legitimate campaign against terrorism. H.T. Imam, a political advisor to Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, indicated that other countries from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) could join Indonesia in applying pressure on Myanmar. Malaysia, another ASEAN member, summoned Myanmar's ambassador to express its concerns regarding the violence and criticized Myanmar for insufficient progress on the issue. Malaysian Foreign Minister Anifah Aman stated that the ongoing violence and discrimination against the Rohingyas should be elevated to a higher international forum. Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who has referred to the violence against Rohingyas as genocide, expressed to Suu Kyi that the situation is of significant concern to the Muslim world and announced that he would send his foreign minister to Bangladesh. Pakistan, which has a substantial Rohingya community, has voiced deep concern over the situation. Approximately 210,000 Rohingya have sought refuge in Bangladesh since October, following smaller attacks by Rohingya insurgents on security posts, which triggered a major counter-offensive by the Myanmar army. Refugees arriving in Shamlapur, along with local residents, reported that hundreds of boats arrived on Monday and Tuesday carrying several thousand individuals. Reuters reporters witnessed men, women, and children disembarking with a few personal belongings, including chickens.
