text: Trump's new travel ban raises bar for legal challenges. NEW YORK/SAN FRANCISCO (Reuters) - The new, more narrowly tailored temporary travel ban President Donald Trump signed on Monday will be more difficult to challenge successfully in court, legal experts said. They noted that since his order no longer covers legal residents or existing visa holders, and makes waivers possible for some business, diplomatic and other travelers, challengers are likely to find it more difficult to identify individuals in the United States who can legally claim they have been harmed, thus establishing the so-called 'standing' to sue. Trump's first executive order signed on Jan. 27 banned travelers from seven Muslim-majority nations - Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen - for 90 days and halted refugee admission for four months, barring Syrian refugees indefinitely. Its rapid implementation caused disruptions and protests at airports. The order faced more than two dozen lawsuits, many alleging discrimination against Muslims. The new ban, which is set to take effect on March 16, removes Iraq from the list and adds categories of individuals who would be exempt from the order. The Trump administration stated that the executive order is necessary for national security reasons. It also specifies groups that could be eligible for waivers, including travelers previously admitted to the United States for work or school, those wishing to visit or reside with a close relative and who would face hardship if denied entry; infants, young children and adoptees or individuals in need of medical care, and employees of the U.S. government and international organizations, among others. All the exceptions make the new order 'a lot harder to attack,' according to Andrew Greenfield, an immigration attorney with Fragomen law firm in Washington D.C. Trump had indicated an intention to make the new directive more resilient to legal challenges, and many of the changes were anticipated. 'They dotted their 'i's' and crossed their 't's' in trying to anticipate what litigation might result,' said Stephen Yale-Loehr, a Cornell Law School professor specializing in immigration. He mentioned that opponents might still identify plaintiffs - a U.S. citizen could potentially sue if the government denies a waiver to their foreign spouse for an arbitrary reason, for instance. In a legal challenge to the original order, the state of Washington successfully prevented its implementation. A federal judge in Seattle and then an appeals court in San Francisco ruled that Washington could claim standing, partly because the order adversely affected legal permanent residents, known as green card holders, in the state. More than 100 businesses, including many prominent tech companies, filed briefs in court arguing that their employees were harmed. Bob Ferguson, the Attorney General for Washington State, indicated on Monday that he would likely decide on the next litigation steps this week after consulting with state universities and businesses about potential harms. 'We need to do our homework and be thoughtful about this,' Ferguson said. The U.S. Department of Justice, in a filing in Seattle federal court on Monday, stated that the new order applies 'only to those who are overseas and without a visa.' Legal experts noted that foreign nationals outside the country who do not have a U.S. visa do not have the same protections under the U.S. Constitution as individuals already present in the country. text: Britain says Moody's downgrade based on 'outdated' Brexit view. LONDON (Reuters) - The British government stated on Friday that the ratings agency Moody's decision to downgrade the country's credit rating was based on an outdated assessment of its plans to leave the European Union. Moody's lowered Britain's sovereign credit rating to Aa2 with a stable outlook from Aa1. A government spokesperson indicated in a statement provided by the finance ministry that the assessments made about Brexit in this report are outdated. Earlier on Friday, Prime Minister Theresa May delivered a speech in Italy outlining her desire for a transition period of approximately two years following Britain's departure from the EU in March 2019. The Prime Minister expressed an ambitious vision for the UK's future relationship with the EU, emphasizing that both parties would benefit from a new and unique partnership, according to the government spokesperson. The spokesperson also noted that substantial progress has been made in reducing the deficit while allocating additional funds for the National Health Service and social care. While acknowledging the challenges ahead, the spokesperson conveyed optimism regarding the future.

text: Republican ex-defense secretary Cohen backs Hillary Clinton. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Former Republican U.S. Defense Secretary William Cohen stated on Wednesday that he is likely to vote for U.S. Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton in the upcoming Nov. 8 U.S. presidential election, citing her experience as secretary of state and former first lady. "In all likelihood, I would say yes," Cohen, who served as defense secretary under former U.S. President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, told MSNBC in an interview when asked if she had earned his vote. "I would not feel comfortable," with Donald Trump, Clinton’s Republican rival and a political novice, having access to the nation’s nuclear codes, Cohen added. "I’d feel more comfortable with Hillary Clinton, certainly," Cohen said during the MSNBC interview.

text: Trump U.S. antitrust nominee says will be independent of White House. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Makan Delrahim, nominated by President Donald Trump to serve as the top U.S. antitrust regulator, stated on Wednesday that he intends to remain independent from the White House while enforcing antitrust law. The Senate is required to vote for Delrahim's confirmation. During a hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, which was influenced by the fallout from Trump’s dismissal of Federal Bureau of Investigation Director James Comey, Delrahim confirmed that he would recuse himself from any involvement regarding the potential merger of health insurer Anthem with rival Cigna. Delrahim had previously worked as a lobbyist for Anthem while employed at the law firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, LLP. The Justice Department under former President Barack Obama filed a lawsuit to prevent the merger, and the case is currently in the appeals process. When questioned about potential discussions with the White House regarding deals under consideration by his division, Delrahim emphasized that antitrust enforcement constitutes law enforcement. He remarked, “The independence of the decisions made in prosecuting and reviewing mergers as well as other conduct is a serious one that should be free from any political influence.” He added, “They will be free if I am fortunate enough to be confirmed.” Currently, Delrahim serves in the White House as deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president. If confirmed, Delrahim’s antitrust division will evaluate corporate mergers at a time when numerous investors and corporate leaders are anticipating a more lenient approach to deal-making. The previous administration encountered a significant number of large mergers, which one enforcer described as a “merger tsunami,” and blocked several of these transactions. Antitrust specialists who have monitored Delrahim’s career expect him to align with the approach of his former supervisor, Hewitt Pate, who held the position of assistant attorney general for antitrust from 2003 to 2005. Delrahim served as Pate’s deputy, focusing on international antitrust matters. Under Pate's leadership, the division faced criticism for permitting too many deals; however, it did initiate lawsuits to prevent the merger of US Airways with United Airlines and to block a combination of DirecTV and EchoStar. It also attempted, but was unsuccessful, in stopping Oracle Corp from acquiring PeopleSoft. If confirmed, Delrahim will oversee the Justice Department’s evaluation of AT&T Inc’s proposal to acquire Time Warner Inc., which owns HBO, Warner Brothers, and news network CNN. The department is also assessing significant transactions in the seeds and agricultural chemicals sector, including the mergers of Dow Chemical Co and Dupont, as well as Bayer and Monsanto. These proposed mergers, along with ChemChina’s acquisition of Syngenta, would reduce the number of agricultural chemical companies from six to three.

text: Ryan opposes Trump working with Democrats on healthcare. In an interview with "CBS This Morning" scheduled to air on Thursday, Ryan articulated his concerns that the Republican Party, which was unable to unify last week to agree on a healthcare reform plan, is urging the president to engage with Democrats in order to fulfill campaign promises to revise Obamacare. "I don’t want that to happen," Ryan stated, in reference to Trump’s proposal to work with Democrats. He characterized the prospect of enacting those reforms with Democratic support as "hardly a conservative thing." Ryan further remarked, "I don’t want government running health care. The government shouldn’t tell you what you must do with your life, with your healthcare." "I think it’s going to happen because we’ve all been promising - Democrat, Republican - we’ve all been promising that to the American people," he stated. text: U.S. Ambassador Haley: U.N. has exhausted options on North Korea. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley stated on Sunday that the U.N. Security Council has exhausted its options for addressing North Korea's nuclear program, suggesting that the United States may need to refer the issue to the Pentagon. "We have pretty much exhausted all the things that we can do at the Security Council at this point," Haley informed CNN's State of the Union, noting her willingness to hand the North Korea issue over to Defense Secretary James Mattis. As world leaders prepare to gather at the United Nations headquarters in New York for the annual General Assembly meeting this week, Haley's remarks signaled that the United States is maintaining its position regarding the potential for military action against North Korea. North Korea conducted a missile launch over Japan into the Pacific Ocean on Thursday, in violation of new U.N. Security Council sanctions that prohibit its textile exports and limit crude oil imports. China has urged the United States to avoid issuing threats to North Korea. Responding to President Donald Trump's warning last month regarding the North Korean threat to the United States, Haley remarked, "It was not an empty threat. If North Korea continues this reckless behavior, and if the United States must defend itself or its allies in any way, North Korea will be destroyed. And we all know that. And none of us want that. None of us want war," she stated on CNN. "We are trying every other possibility that we have, but there are a number of military options on the table," she added. North Korea has launched numerous missiles as it advances its weapons program aimed at achieving the capability to target the United States with a powerful, nuclear-tipped missile. North Korea indicated on Saturday that it seeks to establish an "equilibrium" of military force with the United States. Trump is scheduled to meet with South Korean President Jae-in Moon during the U.N. General Assembly. In a Twitter post on Sunday morning, Trump mentioned, "I spoke with President Moon of South Korea last night. Asked him how Rocket Man is doing. Long gas lines forming in North Korea. Too bad!" White House national security adviser H.R. McMaster stated on Friday, following the latest North Korean missile launch, that the United States is running out of patience: "We’ve been kicking the can down the road, and we’re out of road." On Sunday, he cautioned of imminent danger from Pyongyang: "This regime is so close now to threatening the United States and others with a nuclear weapon, that we really have to move with a great sense of urgency on sanctions, on diplomacy and preparing, if necessary, a military option," McMaster told the Fox News Sunday program. Military options available to Trump include a sea blockade aimed at enforcing sanctions, cruise missile strikes on nuclear and missile facilities, and a broader campaign aimed at overthrowing leader Kim Jong Un. Mattis has indicated that the consequences of any military action could be "tragic on an unbelievable scale" and pose significant risks to U.S. ally South Korea. Democratic U.S. Senator Dianne Feinstein commented on Sunday that Trump should not dismiss the possibility of engaging in talks with North Korea prior to its agreement to terminate its nuclear program. "I think that North Korea is not going to give up its program with nothing on the table," she remarked on CNN. text: Obama tells Latin America and world: give Trump time, don't assume worst. LIMA (Reuters) - U.S. President Barack Obama visited Latin America to address concerns about President-elect Donald Trump, who he previously described as unfit for office. In the final leg of an international farewell tour that included Greece and Germany, Obama sought to alleviate worries following Trump's victory over Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton in the U.S. presidential election. “My main message to you ... and the message I delivered in Europe is don’t just assume the worst,” Obama stated during a question-and-answer session with young people in Peru on Saturday. “Wait until the administration is in place, it’s actually putting its policies together, and then you can make your judgments as to whether or not it’s consistent with the international community’s interest in living in peace and prosperity together.” Trump won the election with promises to build a wall on the U.S.-Mexico border, renegotiate trade agreements, and temporarily ban Muslims from entering the United States. Obama has aimed to reassure the public by committing to a smooth transition of power and expressing hope that Trump would moderate his campaign rhetoric upon taking office. “It will be important for everybody around the world to not make immediate judgments but give this new president-elect a chance to put their team together, to examine the issues, to determine what their policies will be, because as I’ve always said, how you campaign isn’t always the same as how you govern,” Obama said. However, Obama’s reassurances were largely framed in a hopeful context regarding Trump’s potential acceptance of policies endorsed by Democrats, despite Trump’s intention to dismantle them, such as the Iran nuclear agreement and an international climate change pact. The president, who actively supported Clinton and expressed disapproval of Trump, contrasted his statements of reassurance with references to democratic values in Europe and Peru, which Trump has been criticized for neglecting. “You’re seeing some countries that are going backwards rather than forwards in terms of freedom of the press, in terms of freedom of the Internet, in terms of respecting political opposition and civil society,” Obama remarked on Saturday. Trump restricted access for certain news organizations during his campaign and suggested during a televised debate that Clinton could face jail time for her use of a private email server while serving as secretary of state. Although Obama assured European nations that Trump would uphold U.S. commitments to NATO, his other reassurances, particularly concerning Latin American policy, appeared to be based more on optimism than on a comprehensive understanding of Trump’s intentions. “With respect to Latin America, I don’t anticipate major changes in policy from the new administration,” he stated, noting trade as a significant exception. On Friday, Trump made several hawkish appointments for key positions, including attorney general, national security adviser, and CIA director, indicating a possible hardline approach towards Islamist militancy and illegal immigration.

text: South Sudan commander defects to rebels amid showdown with ex-army chief. MOYO, Uganda (Reuters) - A South Sudanese military commander has announced his defection along with more than 200 soldiers to the country's largest rebel group, amid ongoing tensions between President Salva Kiir and his former military chief. Lieutenant Colonel Chan Garang, an ally of former army chief Paul Malong, has joined the largest rebel faction opposing Kiir. All three individuals are ethnic Dinkas, and any division within this influential group may pose a risk to Kiir's leadership. The four-year civil conflict has resulted in the fragmentation of South Sudan into various controlled regions, created Africa's largest refugee crisis in two decades, and led to instances of ethnic cleansing. Approximately one-third of the 12 million population has been displaced from their homes, and half rely on food assistance. In May, Kiir dismissed Malong, who has been accused by U.N. investigators of overseeing ethnic militias responsible for the abuse and murder of civilians. Malong, who is also listed under U.S. sanctions, briefly fled north but returned to the capital, where he has remained under house arrest. Over the weekend, Kiir's forces encircled Malong's residence in Juba and attempted without success to disarm his security personnel. An armed standoff persists outside his home. Garang is the first of Malong's supporters to defect to the rebels. Garang stated that he defected due to the mistreatment of Malong's allies, non-payment of troops for seven months, and discrimination against other tribes. "I left Juba because when you are a supporter of Paul Malong, you will be arrested," Garang communicated to Reuters via satellite phone. "We are preparing our army so that we can launch an attack on Juba. Salva Kiir divided the tribes, so we need him to go." Garang reported taking more than 200 soldiers with him, although a rebel press release cited the number as 150. A photograph provided by the rebels depicted more than 30 armed individuals, though their identities were not confirmed. Army spokesman Lul Ruai Koang stated that they were unaware of any defection from their ranks. Malong was not reachable by phone, but his wife, Lucy Ayak, distanced her husband from the defected commander, saying, "[Garang] is not happy with the government and he has deserted. Why is he saying it is the issue of General Malong?" South Sudan's conflict began in December 2013 between troops loyal to Kiir and rebels led by former vice president Riek Machar, who is a Nuer. Oyet Nathaniel, a senior rebel official, informed Reuters that Garang had brought 150 men with him and that any individual opting to join them against Kiir is a "welcome development," irrespective of their background. There are multiple rebel factions, but none are significantly funded or armed. (This version of the story was refiled to remove repetition in the second to last paragraph.)

text: Erdogan tells Iraqi Kurds they will go hungry if Turkey imposes sanctions. HABUR, Turkey (Reuters) - Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan stated that Iraqi Kurds would face food shortages if Turkey ceases the flow of trucks and oil across the border with northern Iraq. He indicated that all military and economic measures were being considered against its neighbor. These remarks were among the strongest yet from Erdogan regarding the referendum held on Monday in Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region and coincided with Iraqi troops joining the Turkish army for military exercises near Turkey's border with northern Iraq. Initial results suggested significant support for independence; however, Turkey, which has historically served as northern Iraq's primary connection to the outside world, views the referendum as a potential threat to its own security, expressing concern that it may exacerbate separatism among its Kurdish population. Erdogan remarked, "They will be left in the lurch when we start imposing our sanctions." He added, "It will be over when we close the oil taps, all their revenues will vanish, and they will not be able to find food when our trucks stop going to northern Iraq." Turkey, which has the largest Kurdish population in the region, is engaged in a three-decade-long conflict with a Kurdish insurgency in its southeast, adjacent to northern Iraq. Erdogan noted that traffic was currently only permitted to cross from Turkey into Iraq. While he has consistently threatened economic sanctions, he has provided limited specifics. According to IMF data, hundreds of thousands of barrels of oil per day are transported through a pipeline in Turkey from northern Iraq to global oil markets. In 2016, Iraq, including the Kurdish region, was Turkey's third-largest export market, with total exports amounting to $8.6 billion, following Germany and the United Kingdom. Erdogan stated that all potential measures, including economic and military actions involving land and air space, were under consideration, asserting that Iraqi Kurds lack the capability to establish a state. "They don’t have an idea on how to be a state. They think that they are a state just by saying it. This can’t and won’t happen," he said. Iraqi soldiers participated in military exercises with Turkish troops in southeast Turkey near the border with Iraq on Tuesday, as reported by a Reuters witness, as the two countries align their responses to the referendum. A small group of soldiers carrying both Iraqi and Turkish flags traversed the dusty plain where the exercises, initiated the previous week, were taking place 4 km (2.5 miles) from the Habur border gate. The flags were displayed from the top of an armored personnel carrier. National and international media observed the exercises from the main highway leading to the border gate. Erdogan also accused Masoud Barzani, the president of the Kurdistan Regional Government, of acting with treachery regarding the vote. "Until the very last moment, we weren’t expecting Barzani to make such a mistake as holding the referendum. Apparently we were wrong," Erdogan stated. "This referendum decision, which has been taken without any consultation, is treachery."

text: Trump's low approval rating masks his support among likely voters: Reuters/Ipsos poll. NEW YORK (Reuters) - According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, President Donald Trump enjoys greater popularity among likely voters than he does with the general public. This finding may explain why many Republican lawmakers have continued to support the president despite his declining approval ratings. The poll, released on Wednesday, indicates that Trump receives higher approval ratings from individuals who participated in the 2016 presidential election compared to the overall U.S. adult population, which includes both voters and non-voters. Approximately 60 percent of the voting-age public participated in last year’s election. In October, for instance, 44 percent of 2016 voters expressed approval of Trump’s performance in office, as opposed to 37 percent of the general population. Among Republicans, 82 percent of voters approved of Trump in October, compared to 75 percent of all Republicans. (Graphic: tmsnrt.rs/2zoIC1A) The poll also found that 85 percent of those who voted for Trump in 2016 would do so again. These findings suggest that Republican candidates in the 2018 congressional elections who distance themselves from the president may risk alienating his supporters, according to Republican strategists and political scientists. Conversely, candidates who align themselves with Trump in early primary races may face challenges in appealing to moderate voters in the general election. Michael McDonald, a voter turnout expert at the University of Florida, noted the difficulty for any Republican candidate to separate themselves from Trump. This dilemma was evident in Virginia on Tuesday, where Ed Gillespie, the Republican candidate for governor, was defeated by his Democratic opponent. Gillespie had adopted some of Trump’s hardline positions but did not campaign alongside the president. His strategy was observed closely within the party to determine if it could serve as a model for other Republican candidates in 2018, when control of the House of Representatives and the Senate will be contested. Gillespie’s loss led to discussions among Republicans about their future strategy on Wednesday. Trump suggested in a tweet that the outcome might have differed had Gillespie fully embraced him, while critics noted that exit polls indicated a third of Virginian voters turned out to express discontent with Trump, which is double the number who voted to show support for the president. The results from Tuesday indicate that opposition to Trump has increased, even as he retains popularity among voters from the 2016 election, said Elaine Kamarck, a presidential politics expert at the Brookings Institution. Kamarck commented that for Republicans, the challenge will not be mobilizing their base but rather attracting additional voters in elections where Republican support is outnumbered. Reuters/Ipsos conducted its analysis by generating two separate surveys: one targeted at voters and another at the general public. For the voter poll, Reuters/Ipsos re-engaged individuals who participated in its exit poll on Nov. 8, 2016, the day of the U.S. presidential election. Those voters received follow-up questionnaires in May, July, and October, inquiring about their approval or disapproval of the president. The responses were subsequently compared to data from a separate survey – the Reuters/Ipsos national tracking poll – which assesses the opinions of all adults in the United States. In May and July, results from both polls were quite similar, with around 40 percent of voters and the general adult population indicating approval for the president. However, by October, the polls diverged, revealing that voters expressed stronger levels of approval than the general public. Jan Leighley, a political behavior expert at American University, stated that it is reasonable to conclude that Trump is more popular among those who participated in the 2016 election due to demographic factors, as they were more likely to be white and less likely to identify with Democrats than the general population.

text: Four U.S. lawmakers have called on the country's auto safety regulators to initiate a comprehensive effort to mitigate potential hacking threats to vehicle computer systems. In a letter sent to the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) on Monday, the Republican representatives expressed their concerns regarding the vulnerability of vehicles to cyberattacks. Although there have been no confirmed incidents of vehicle hacking, studies have indicated that remote access to critical vehicle functions, including car horns, brakes, and power steering, is feasible. The correspondence referenced research published in August by Wired magazine, which detailed how two researchers successfully manipulated a 2014 Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV Jeep SUV, causing it to behave in an “erratic and unsafe manner” through the vehicle's on-board diagnostics (OBD) port. This port has been a requirement in all vehicles since 1994 for emissions testing. The letter, authored by Representative Fred Upton of Michigan, who chairs the House Energy and Commerce Committee, along with three other lawmakers, noted that the current design of the OBD port poses an increasing risk to passenger safety and security. In response to the Wired article, Fiat Chrysler stated that the demonstration necessitated a computer to be physically connected to the vehicle's port and cautioned vehicle owners against connecting unknown or untrusted devices to the OBD port. NHTSA has not yet provided a response to the letter. The agency has announced plans to issue cybersecurity guidelines for the auto industry in the near future. The U.S. government is addressing this concern, as evidenced by the Justice Department's recent formation of a threat analysis team dedicated to examining national security risks associated with self-driving cars, medical devices, and other internet-connected technologies. Additionally, the Federal Bureau of Investigation and NHTSA released a bulletin in March indicating that motor vehicles are becoming increasingly susceptible to hacking.

text: Voice of triumph or doom: North Korean presenter back in limelight for nuclear test. SEOUL (Reuters) - Television presenter Ri Chun Hee reported on Pyongyang's sixth nuclear test while wearing a pink Korean dress. With her characteristic delivery, Ri announced on state television on Sunday that the hydrogen bomb test was a perfect success and a significant step in completing the state nuclear force. The 74-year-old grandmother has been a prominent figure since she began her career in broadcasting in 1971, transitioning from acting to join Korean Central Television (KCTV). Her dramatic style distinguishes her from other presenters, whether she is condemning the West or highlighting the regime's accomplishments and the strength of its leaders. Ahn Chan-il, a North Korean defector now residing in South Korea, commented on her unique vocal power, stating, "There is no one else who has that power in her voice as she does. It’s just right for talking about nuclear weapons or missiles." Ri, typically seen in a traditional Korean dress known as a hanbok, has also displayed a more emotional side. She was seen crying on air when she announced the death of North Korea's founder, Kim Il Sung, in 1994. When his son, Kim Jong Il, died in 2011, it was Ri, dressed in black funeral attire and with a trembling voice, who conveyed the news to the North Korean people. Although she officially retired in 2012, Ri has been called back for significant announcements. The broadcast on Sunday highlighted her enduring presence at a time when current leader Kim Jong Un has removed several officials from his father's era. Outside North Korea, Ri is recognized as a prominent figure of the regime amid ongoing tensions surrounding Pyongyang's weapons programs. Tokyo resident Masashi Sakota remarked that he expected her to speak if any major developments occurred. Matt Walker, a credit manager in Sydney, noted that Ri appeared very expressive and enthusiastic during the news item he viewed this week, stating, "I don’t know how you can get excited about bombs going off. In a rare 2012 interview with China's state-run CCTV, Ri expressed a desire to help mentor the next generation of North Korean broadcasters, whom she regarded as better suited for contemporary audiences. She indicated that she reserved her gentler demeanor for the North Korean public, explaining, "When we read to people in the DPRK, you shouldn’t shout but speak gently to viewers." text: U.S. intelligence agencies are currently in disagreement with Republican members of Congress regarding access to a classified CIA report that determined Russia hacked Democratic Party data to assist Donald Trump in winning the presidency. Republican lawmakers have expressed frustration over Director of National Intelligence James Clapper’s refusal to grant full briefings to Congress' two intelligence committees. According to U.S. government officials, the leadership of Congress and the chairpersons of the two intelligence committees, referred to as the “Gang of Eight,” have received briefings on the CIA's findings. Representative Devin Nunes, a California Republican and chair of the House Intelligence Committee, who is also a member of President-elect Trump’s transition team and the Gang of Eight, has requested a briefing for his full committee regarding the CIA assessment. Nunes stated, "The committee is vigorously looking into reports of cyber-attacks during the election campaign, and in particular we want to clarify press reports that the CIA has a new assessment that it has not shared with us." Representative Ron Johnson, chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, noted that his committee has also sought a briefing, which the CIA declined. Johnson commented, "It is disappointing that the CIA would provide information on this issue to the Washington Post and NBC but will not provide information to elected members of Congress." Three U.S. government sources, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss classified information, informed Reuters that while the full congressional committees have not been briefed, congressional leadership has been briefed, which is standard procedure for sensitive intelligence matters. The sources indicated that Nunes had received personal briefings on the CIA's conclusions, though a congressional official refuted this claim. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) stated that President Barack Obama ordered a comprehensive review of foreign efforts to influence U.S. presidential elections from 2008 to the present, and therefore, agencies would refrain from further comments until this review is completed. According to the ODNI, which oversees all 16 U.S. intelligence agencies, the intelligence community will be prepared to brief Congress once the review is finished and will make the study available to the public while protecting intelligence sources and methods. The CIA's conclusion regarding Russian hacking is based not on irrefutable evidence but primarily on the observation that Russians hacked both political parties but only disseminated information detrimental to Democrats and their presidential candidate, Hillary Clinton, according to a U.S. official familiar with the CIA's work, who requested anonymity. Two government sources reported on Friday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation now supports the CIA's assessment that the Russian hacks were intended to benefit Trump's campaign. All three sources indicated that the ODNI concurs with this assessment. The FBI had not issued an immediate comment. Initially, the FBI, which manages counterintelligence investigations within the U.S., did not endorse the CIA's finding as it did not meet the evidentiary standards required for a conviction in a U.S. court or identify individuals responsible for the hacking that violated American law, according to one source. The ongoing debate over Russian hacking is also creating tensions between Trump and certain Republican lawmakers. The president-elect has continued to downplay the intelligence agencies’ conclusion that Russian President Vladimir Putin directed the hacking. On Friday, Senator Richard Burr, Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, announced that his committee will conduct a review in the upcoming year.

text: Bangladesh, Myanmar agree to draw up plan for refugee repatriation: minister. DHAKA (Reuters) - Bangladesh and Myanmar agreed on Monday to establish a working group to plan the repatriation of more than half a million Rohingya Muslim refugees who have fled to Bangladesh due to an army crackdown, according to the Bangladeshi foreign minister. The United Nations has described the exodus of 507,000 Rohingya since late August as the world’s fastest-developing refugee emergency, asserting that Buddhist-majority Myanmar is engaging in ethnic cleansing against its Rohingya Muslim minority. Myanmar has denied these claims, stating that its forces are combating Rohingya terrorists who initiated the recent violence with coordinated attacks on security forces on August 25. Myanmar reports that over 500 individuals have been killed since then, most of whom are insurgents accused of attacking civilians and igniting the fires that have destroyed more than half of over 400 Rohingya villages in northern Rakhine State. Bangladesh Foreign Minister Abul Hassan Mahmood Ali confirmed that he and Myanmar official Kyaw Tint Swe had reached an agreement to form the working group to create repatriation plans. Ali expressed a desire for a peaceful resolution to the crisis. Kyaw Tint Swe did not provide comments to the media, and government representatives in Myanmar were not immediately available for further comment. Rohingya have sought refuge in Bangladesh over the years, citing persecution, particularly during the late 1970s, early 1990s, and in October of the previous year, following smaller insurgent attacks on security forces. Although the two countries have previously agreed on repatriation plans, the core issue regarding the status of Rohingya in Myanmar remains unresolved. The Rohingya are denied citizenship and classified as illegal immigrants, despite asserting historical ties to Myanmar that extend back centuries, and communities have faced marginalization and episodes of communal violence over the years. When asked about the limited impact of past agreements, Ali stated, "This time we want to be hopeful." In Geneva, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Filippo Grandi noted that the issues of statelessness must be addressed, emphasizing that the connection between statelessness and displacement is particularly evident in the case of the Rohingya community. The situation regarding the treatment of the Rohingya represents a significant challenge for Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who has been in office since forming a government last year after winning a notable election in 2015. In an address to the nation last month, the Nobel peace laureate indicated that Myanmar was prepared to initiate a verification process based on a 1993 agreement with Bangladesh, stating that refugees from this country would be accepted without any issues. However, many refugees express concerns about their ability to provide the necessary documentation that Myanmar may require to validate their right to return. Myanmar has not permitted access to a U.N. fact-finding mission, but Suu Kyi appointed a team led by former U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan last year to provide recommendations for addressing issues in Rakhine. The commission submitted its recommendations on August 24, one day prior to the insurgent attacks, which included a review of a law linking citizenship to ethnicity, leaving most Rohingya stateless. The panel also suggested that the government take action against rights violations, ensure freedom of movement, and invest in infrastructure to alleviate poverty in the state. In her recent address, Suu Kyi reiterated her commitment to these recommendations. Prior to the latest exodus, there were already approximately 300,000 Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh. In an effort to portray the situation, the Myanmar government escorted a group of diplomats and senior U.N. officials to Rakhine. Swiss ambassador Paul Seger remarked on Twitter that Maungdaw felt like a ghost town upon his arrival in the main town of northern Rakhine. Myanmar has restricted access to the area.

text: Trump's body language during debate raises social media eyebrows. NEW YORK (Reuters) - U.S. Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump paced, frowned and physically loomed at times over Democratic rival Hillary Clinton during Sunday night’s town-hall debate, prompting reactions on social media. The online response highlighted the contentious nature of the encounter in St. Louis, where Trump and Clinton exchanged insults less than a month before the Nov. 8 U.S. presidential election. Twitter users commented on Trump’s body language, with some indicating that he appeared to have followed Clinton around the stage. The criticism arose as Trump faced scrutiny following the release of a 2005 videotape featuring lewd and demeaning remarks about women. “#Trump’s body language [was] bizarre,” wrote Twitter user Sheena (@texdakota). “Pacing, insulting, standing right behind her.” “Trump’s body language freaked me out,” wrote Charlotte (@charlotteirene8). “I get very uncomfortable when men stand behind me, especially like that.” A spokeswoman for Trump did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Clinton’s performance also received online criticism. “Clinton could have done better,” tweeted ryank (@ryantkelly). “Didn’t seem as hungry, as able to get under his skin tonight.” Sentiment on Trump’s performance was 66.9 percent negative, according to an analysis by social intelligence firm Brandwatch of Twitter posts during the debate, while Clinton’s was 57.8 percent negative. The debate, featuring questions from audience members, was the most tweeted-about debate ever, with more than 17 million tweets, according to Twitter spokesman Nick Pacilio. Trump’s statement that he and running mate Mike Pence differed on their approach to military intervention in Syria was noted as the most-discussed moment of the night on the microblogging site.

text: Pentagon notified U.S. Congress of $593 million military sale to Nigeria. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Pentagon has notified the U.S. Congress of the sale to Nigeria of 12 Super Tucano A-29 planes and weapons worth $593 million, which the West African country seeks for its efforts against the militant group Boko Haram. The Federal Register on Monday published the Aug. 2 notification from the Pentagon’s Defense Security Cooperation Agency. The sale includes thousands of bombs and rockets and was originally agreed upon by former President Barack Obama’s administration. The Super Tucano A-29 is an agile, propeller-driven aircraft with reconnaissance, surveillance, and attack capabilities, manufactured by Brazil’s Embraer. A second production line is located in Florida, in collaboration with Embraer and privately held Sierra Nevada Corp of Sparks, Nevada. The Super Tucano costs more than $10 million each, and the price may increase based on the configuration. It is powered by a Pratt & Whitney Canada PT 6 engine. The Obama administration postponed the deal following incidents, including the Nigerian Air Force’s bombing of a refugee camp in January that resulted in the deaths of 90 to 170 civilians. President Donald Trump has indicated his intention to proceed with foreign defense sales that were delayed under Obama due to human rights concerns. (This story corrects headline and paragraphs 1 and 2 to reflect that the notification was made on Aug. 2, not on Monday)

text: WHO urges Trump to expand Obamacare, ensure healthcare for all. GENEVA (Reuters) - The World Health Organization (WHO) on Friday urged U.S. President-elect Donald Trump to expand Obamacare and ensure all Americans have access to healthcare. The real estate magnate takes office next month after promising to repeal outgoing President Barack Obama’s signature healthcare policy, which has provided medical insurance to millions of Americans but has faced criticism from Republican lawmakers. Agnes Soucat, the WHO’s director of health system governance and financing, indicated that there are various methods to provide health coverage to a larger population, emphasizing that it relates to "political choices." "We as the WHO really encourage the new administration to make sure that the social contract is expanded and that all U.S. citizens have access to health care," Soucat stated during a news briefing in Geneva. The United States is the only country among the 35 member states of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) that does not offer universal health care, which is a primary objective of the U.N. Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, according to Soucat. The Affordable Care Act, commonly referred to as Obamacare, has extended health coverage to approximately 25 million previously uninsured Americans. Critics from the Republican Party argue that it has introduced unnecessary government involvement in personal healthcare and the private sector. In late November, Trump appointed Republican U.S. Representative Tom Price, an orthopedic surgeon from Georgia and a critic of Obamacare, to serve as his health secretary. Price has advocated for a proposal that includes tax credits, expanded health savings accounts, and reforms to lawsuits as potential alternatives to Obamacare. The Republican Party is experiencing divisions regarding the timeline for repealing Obamacare, with some members suggesting that a delay would allow for the development of a replacement plan, preventing millions of Americans from losing their health insurance without an alternative. "There are different strategies to make universal health care particularly pro-poor," Soucat noted. "So what we are saying is, yes, this would be a setback if people would lose coverage."

text: Shots fired at DMZ as North Korean soldier defects to South. SEOUL (Reuters) - South Korean guards fired warning shots across the heavily militarized border with North Korea on Thursday as a soldier from the North defected in thick fog, complicating efforts to ease tensions over Pyongyang's nuclear and missile programs. A South Korean defense ministry official stated that up to 20 warning shots were fired as North Korean troops approached too near the military demarcation line at the demilitarized zone (DMZ), apparently in search of the missing soldier. Thursday's defection occurred about five weeks after a North Korean soldier suffered critical gunshot wounds during a defection dash across the border. Additionally, two North Korean civilians were found in a fishing boat on Wednesday and had sought to defect, according to officials in the South. This brings the total number of North Koreans who have defected by taking dangerous routes either directly across the border or by sea to 15 so far this year, including two other soldiers. This figure represents three times the number from last year, according to South Korean officials. Tensions on the Korean peninsula were already elevated after North Korea accelerated testing of its missile and nuclear programs this year in defiance of international pressure and UN sanctions. The defections may also complicate South Korea's efforts to ensure the smooth running of the 2018 Winter Olympics, which begin in Pyeongchang in February. South Korean President Moon Jae-in said on Tuesday he had proposed postponing major military drills with the United States until after the games in an attempt to improve relations, although officials in Seoul later indicated that any proposed delay would depend on the North not engaging in any provocations. In a notice published online, the U.S. military's 8th Army stated that a significant number of North Korean propaganda leaflets and CDs had been distributed at strategic locations on multiple U.S. military bases in South Korea. The notice urged troops to report any suspicious individuals to help combat potential insider threats that could disrupt military operations. The United States stations 28,500 troops in South Korea, a legacy of the 1950-53 Korean War, and North Korea claims that regular U.S.-South Korean military drills are a prelude to invasion. It frequently threatens to destroy the United States and its two key Asian allies, South Korea and Japan. Seoul reports that more than 880 North Koreans have defected to the democratic South so far this year, but the majority have taken a less dangerous route through China. Traveling through China, North Korea's neighbor and sole major ally, allows them to avoid the DMZ, which features landmines, barbed wire, surveillance cameras, electric fencing, and thousands of armed troops on both sides. The number of defectors arriving successfully in the South has decreased since North Korean leader Kim Jong Un took power in late 2011, a trend linked by defectors and experts to a crackdown by Pyongyang. There was no immediate comment from the secretive North regarding the latest incidents. However, North Korean state media released a statement sharply denying U.S. allegations this week that Pyongyang was responsible for a number of recent cyber attacks. Washington has publicly attributed a cyber attack in May that affected hospitals, banks, and other companies to North Korean hackers. Researchers also suggest that North Korea was likely involved in attacks on virtual currency exchanges. The military drills with the United States have further complicated relations with China. The proposed delay in drills was discussed during a summit between Moon and Chinese President Xi Jinping last week after the proposal was submitted to Washington, an official at the presidential Blue House stated this week. China and Russia have proposed a freeze for freeze arrangement under which North Korea would cease its nuclear and missile tests in exchange for a halt to the exercises, but there has been little progress.

text: Billionaire Branson targeted in $5 million scam. LONDON (Reuters) - Richard Branson, billionaire founder of the Virgin group, has disclosed that he was the target of a fraudster impersonating Britain’s defense minister who attempted to solicit $5 million from him for a purported secret ransom payment. In a request for assistance in identifying the individual, Branson indicated that he believed the same conman subsequently impersonated him to defraud a friend of $2 million by falsely claiming to raise funds for those affected by Hurricane Irma. Branson described the situation as reminiscent of a narrative from a John le Carre novel or a James Bond film, though he confirmed it was factual. Recognized for his wavy blond hair and beard, Branson is among Britain's prominent businessmen. The Virgin brand extends across various sectors, including airlines, train services, telecommunications, and fitness. Branson recounted that six months prior, following an elaborate setup involving a note on counterfeit government letterhead, he received a phone call from an individual claiming to be Defence Secretary Michael Fallon. The caller informed Branson that a British diplomat had been kidnapped and was being held for ransom by terrorists. He asserted that while the government typically does not pay ransoms, there was a sensitive rationale for the diplomat's release, and a group of British business people was being confidentially solicited for assistance. Branson was asked to contribute $5 million toward the ransom, with assurances that the British government would reimburse him. Upon feeling uneasy, Branson verified with government officials and was informed that Fallon had not communicated with him. The incident was subsequently reported to the police. Six months later, Branson learned that a friend, a successful businessman in the United States, had received a call from a conman impersonating him. During the call, the impersonator convincingly mimicked Branson's voice and fabricated a story about urgently needing a loan while he was attempting to provide aid in the British Virgin Islands (BVI). Branson, who owns a small island in the BVI, had previously been public about the devastation caused by Hurricane Irma in that region. The caller exploited this context, alleging that he could not reach his bank in the UK due to communication issues with Europe and that he had only just managed to make a satellite call to the American businessman. The individual, described as extremely gracious, provided $2 million, which subsequently disappeared. A spokesman for Fallon stated that he was aware of two attempts, one unrelated to Branson, to impersonate the minister for illicit purposes, and that Fallon’s office was cooperating with police efforts to apprehend those responsible.

text: Spain issues arrest warrant for ousted Catalan leader. MADRID/BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Spain on Friday issued an arrest warrant on sedition and other charges against Carles Puigdemont, following the dismissal of his government after a declaration of independence. A judge from the Madrid High Court requested that Belgium arrest Puigdemont and four associates after they failed to comply with a court order to return to Spain on Thursday to address charges of rebellion, sedition, misuse of public funds, disobedience, and breach of trust related to their secessionist campaign. The judge denied a request from Puigdemont to give testimony via video conference from Belgium. In Brussels, a federal prosecutor stated that Belgian authorities would review the warrant before presenting it to a judge. Eric Van der Sypt informed Reuters that the warrant would be submitted to an investigative judge possibly by tomorrow or the day after. Puigdemont, who is contemplating running in a snap election in the region on December 21, has expressed distrust towards the Spanish justice system but indicated a willingness to cooperate with the Belgian courts. Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy, amidst Spain's most significant political crisis since the late 1970s, called for elections after taking control of Catalonia in response to last week's declaration of independence by its parliament. Belgium has up to three months to decide whether to extradite Puigdemont back to Spain, as a European arrest warrant may be blocked for several procedural reasons. On Thursday, nine members of Puigdemont's dismissed cabinet were ordered by the High Court to remain in custody pending investigation and potential trial. Puigdemont stated on Belgian state television RTBF on Friday, "We consider ourselves a legitimate government. There must be a continuity to tell the world what’s going on in Spain. It’s not with a government in jail that the elections will be neutral, independent, normal. I am ready to be a candidate; it’s possible to run a campaign from anywhere." The detention of the secessionist leaders and Puigdemont's arrival in Belgium have reinvigorated the secessionist movement following previous divisions. In response to the detentions, Catalan civic groups Asamblea Nacional Catalana and Omnium Cultural, whose leaders were imprisoned last month on sedition charges, have called for a general strike on November 8 and a mass demonstration on November 11. Another six Catalan leaders are scheduled to testify on the same charges on November 9. One member of the dismissed cabinet, Santi Vila, was released on Friday after posting bail of 50,000 euros ($58,300). The other eight members may remain in custody for up to four years. Vila resigned from the Catalan cabinet prior to the independence declaration, and while he supports secession, he has advocated for a negotiated resolution with the central government. He has expressed interest in becoming the leading candidate for Puigdemont's PdeCat (Catalan Democratic party) in the regional election. Thousands participated in pro-independence demonstrations on Thursday night across several Catalan towns, and parties in the current coalition Junts Pel Si (Together For Yes) are seeking to run again on a unified ticket in the election. An opinion poll released on Tuesday indicated that Junts Pel Si would secure 35.2 percent of the vote if the election were held immediately and could potentially achieve a parliamentary majority if it maintains its alliance with the far-left party CUP. The Spanish government announced on Friday its intention to engage in legal discussions with those holding a majority. Foreign Affairs Minister Alfonso Dastis conveyed to French newspaper Le Figaro that the government could offer new dialogue to address Catalans' aspirations for increased autonomy and consider constitutional reforms, including the potential for a federal model to grant regions more autonomy, including financial autonomy.

text: Putin's Syria envoy: U.S. forces should leave Syria. ASTANA (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy for Syria stated on Thursday that there was no justification for U.S. forces to remain in Syria and that the reasons provided by Washington for maintaining a military presence there were unfounded. Alexander Lavrentiev made these remarks in Astana, the capital of Kazakhstan, prior to a new round of Syrian peace talks involving Russia, Iran, and Turkey. Lavrentiev noted that the Astana discussions would aim to establish the groundwork for a Congress of Syrian Peoples that Russia intends to host early next year. The parties involved plan to determine the date for the congress on Friday, according to his statements. However, reaching an agreement on a list of delegates is expected to take longer, potentially up to three weeks. Turkey expressed objections last month regarding the participation of the primary Syrian Kurdish group in the congress.

text: Kenya court to rule on presidential election cases on Monday. text: Turkish academics to be tried in April over Kurdish letter. ISTANBUL (Reuters) - A Turkish court on Tuesday adjourned for four months the trial of 10 academics who signed a letter to the Turkish government last year calling for violence against Turkey's Kurds to end. The academics are the first group from 148 who are being prosecuted for signing the open letter. They are accused of insulting the Turkish government and carrying out propaganda for a terrorist group. In total, 1,128 academics from Turkey and abroad, including philosopher and activist Noam Chomsky, signed the January 2016 letter, titled "We will not be a party to this crime!" It called for an end to violence in Kurdish-majority towns in eastern Turkey, which escalated after the collapse in 2015 of a ceasefire between the Turkish government and the militant Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK). In the letter, published a few months after the violence erupted, they said the Turkish state was condemning residents in the mainly Kurdish southeastern provinces to hunger through its use of curfews that have been ongoing for weeks. It also accused authorities of deploying heavy weapons that should only be used in war. "We demand the government to prepare the conditions for negotiations and create a road map that would lead to a lasting peace which includes the demands of the Kurdish political movement," it said. Tuesday's hearing, against six academics from Galatasaray University and four from Istanbul University, was adjourned to April 12 after the court rejected the lawyers' submission that the letter was a criticism of the government, not an insult. Criticizing the government is not punishable under Turkey's penal code, while insulting it is. A defense lawyer for three academics from Istanbul University stated, "It is obvious, from a legal standpoint, that there is no crime here, but, politically, (the authorities) want to turn it into something else." The PKK took up arms in 1984 and more than 40,000 people have died in the conflict since then. The group is considered a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. The academics published their letter six months before last year's failed military coup. Since then, thousands of academics have been fired for alleged links to terrorist organizations. Some academics express concern that Turkey's progress in academia in recent years is now in jeopardy. Rights groups accuse President Tayyip Erdogan of using a state of emergency declared after the coup to quash political dissent.

text: Cuba holds municipal elections on road to Castro era’s end. HAVANA (Reuters) - Cuba took another step on Sunday toward the end of the Castro era, with millions of residents placing paper ballots in cardboard boxes for ward delegates to municipal assemblies. The vote comes the day after the first anniversary of revolutionary leader Fidel Castro's death and precedes another election early next year for provincial and national assembly deputies. The new national assembly, where 50 percent of the deputies must be ward delegates elected on Sunday, is expected on Feb. 24 to select a new president to replace Raul Castro, Fidel's 86-year-old younger brother, who has said he will step down after serving two five-year terms. The Castro brothers have headed the government since the 1959 revolution. Raul Castro will remain head of the Communist Party until 2021, the only legal party in Cuba. Nearly 27,000 candidates are running for 12,515 ward positions in Sunday's election, the only part of the electoral process that is contested publicly and with direct participation by ordinary Cubans. The results will be announced on Monday. The candidates for the provincial and national assemblies are nominated by commissions composed of representatives of Communist Party-controlled organizations, such as the trade union federation, then presented as a slate for a public vote. Those slates have had the same number of names as seats in previous elections. Fifty percent of those names must be ward delegates. The electoral cycle comes at a tricky time for the Caribbean nation as the revolutionary generation passes, an economic reform program appears stalled, aid from key ally Venezuela shrinks, and the Trump administration threatens. Yet candidates debated none of these issues before Sunday's vote. First Vice President Miguel Diaz-Canel, who is expected to succeed Castro, lauded the electoral process and refused to speculate about his future. 'Today is a day to talk about what we are doing and Fidel,' he told reporters after casting his ballot. Asked about relations with the United States, he said Cuba remained interested in improving them but reiterated its position that negotiations would have to be based on mutual respect and equality and without dictates. 'The future depends on them, not us,' he said. Campaigning is prohibited in Cuba, and candidates for the ward posts were nominated at neighborhood meetings based on their personal merits, not policy positions. They need not belong to the Communist Party, and many candidates are independents, but only a few government opponents have ever competed. 'I am happy to vote, but I must say, like most young people I do not think it makes any difference,' said a young woman, who requested anonymity because she holds an important government job. She added that there was an ongoing discussion on how to reform the electoral process and make government more responsive. This year a coalition of opposition groups ran more than 160 pre-candidates, but most were blocked by state security from nomination meetings, and none are running on Sunday.

text: U.S. observing rise in piracy off Somalia, links to famine. DJIBOUTI (Reuters) - The United States is monitoring a recent increase in piracy off the coast of Somalia, a senior U.S. military official stated on Sunday during Defense Secretary Jim Mattis' visit to a military base in Djibouti. The rise in piracy attacks has been attributed in part to famine and drought in the region, as indicated by the top U.S. military commander overseeing troops in Africa during Mattis’ visit as part of a week-long trip to the Middle East and Africa. The United States utilizes the base in Djibouti, a small country comparable in size to Wales located at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, as a launch point for operations in Yemen and Somalia. The recent series of attacks by Somali pirates follows a lengthy period without reported incidents. Attacks peaked at 237 in 2011 but declined sharply afterward as ship owners enhanced security measures and international naval forces increased patrols. This month has witnessed a resurgence of attacks, with two ships captured and a third rescued by Indian and Chinese forces after the crew requested assistance and secured themselves in a safe room. "The bottom line is there have been a half dozen or so incidents," Marine General Thomas Waldhauser noted at a press conference alongside Mattis. "We’re not ready to say there is a trend there yet but we’ll continue to watch," he remarked, adding that one factor contributing to the increase was famine and droughts in the region, as some targeted vessels were transporting food and oil. According to the U.N. World Food Programme, over 20 million people from Nigeria, Somalia, South Sudan, and Yemen face the risk of starvation within the next six months. In South Sudan alone, more than 100,000 individuals are experiencing famine, with an additional million on the verge of starvation. Mattis indicated that while the situation is being monitored, he does not anticipate a U.S. military response to the increase in piracy. A U.S. defense official, speaking anonymously, mentioned that international shipping companies may have become complacent regarding their security, which could also account for the rise in piracy incidents. Djibouti holds strategic significance as it lies on the route to the Suez Canal. The nation, bordered by Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Somalia, also hosts Japanese and French military bases. The U.S. base, which has approximately 4,000 personnel, is located close to a Chinese base that is still under construction, raising concerns among some U.S. officials. Mattis’ visit to the base coincides with the United States intensifying pressure on militant groups such as al Shabaab in the region. The White House recently granted the U.S. military broader authority to engage al Qaeda-linked al Shabaab militants in Somalia. Waldhauser informed reporters that he has not yet utilized the new authorities provided by the White House. Al Shabaab has managed to conduct lethal bombings despite losing most of its territory to African Union peacekeepers supporting the Somali government. On Sunday, a military vehicle was struck by a roadside bomb in Somalia’s semi-autonomous Puntland region, resulting in the deaths of at least six soldiers and injuring another eight. The United States has recently deployed a few dozen troops to Somalia to assist in training members of the Somali National Army. It is also conducting strikes in Yemen against al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP). AQAP is known for having one of the world’s most dangerous bomb makers, Ibrahim Hassan al-Asiri, and has remained a persistent concern for the U.S. government since a 2009 attempt to detonate a bomb on a Detroit-bound airliner on Christmas Day.

text: One dead at protest against extending Ugandan president's rule. KAMPALA (Reuters) - At least one person has died as police used bullets and teargas to disperse a crowd of opposition supporters on Wednesday who were rallying against plans to extend Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni's rule. Police have intervened to break up a series of protests in recent days regarding a bill that would allow the 73-year-old president to stand for election again in 2021, despite the current constitutional age limit for candidates being set at 75. Rights organizations and activists have expressed concern over similar actions by other long-serving leaders in Africa, including those in Rwanda, Burundi, and Burkina Faso, who have sought to extend their terms. Police spokesman Elly Maate reported that one individual died after officers fired bullets into the air to disperse a crowd that was gathering for what was described as an illegal rally near a stadium in the southwestern town of Rukungiri. Opposition party member Ingrid Turinawe and a local government official indicated that two men had died. Turinawe further stated that a bullet struck a vehicle carrying opposition leader Kizza Besigye. Although he was unharmed, an image displayed a significant hole in the rear window of his vehicle. A legislator aligned with Museveni introduced the bill to remove the presidential age limit last month. Museveni met with members of parliament supporting the measure last week, during which he publicly expressed his support for the legislation, according to reports from several local media outlets.

text: Trump's war chest one of smallest in recent presidential campaigns. WASHINGTON/NEW YORK (Reuters) - Republican Donald Trump may be among the least well-funded presidential candidates in recent history, entering the final month of the election lacking the financial resources needed to match the staffing and advertising levels that have benefited his Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton. With less than three weeks remaining until the election, it is unlikely that Trump can significantly increase his funding to launch a spending campaign that could alter the trajectory of his campaign. By the end of September, Trump had raised a total of $163 million, compared to Clinton’s $449 million. Trump, a New York real estate developer known for his wealth, has committed to using millions of his personal assets to support his campaign. In addition to the $163 million raised, he contributed $47.5 million during the primary and an additional $8.6 million later. Trump's fundraising challenges stem from a series of campaign difficulties that have made affluent donors hesitant to support him, and he has shown a reluctance to engage in fundraising activities or solicit large donations. This presents a notable disadvantage for Trump, as evidenced by his spending in key areas such as staffing and television advertisements ahead of the November 8 election. Regarding staff, Trump has expended $5 million, while Clinton has allocated approximately $38 million. As of September, Trump employed 168 individuals, an increase from the 82 he had in July. Trump also spent $5 million on field consultants, who are not part of the core staff, whereas Clinton employed 815 individuals in September. In terms of advertising, Trump has spent $48.7 million compared to Clinton’s expenditure of $204 million, allowing her to saturate the media with advertisements. This financial advantage has enabled Clinton to invest additional funds in states that have become more competitive as Election Day approaches. Recently, Clinton's campaign announced an extra $2 million expenditure in Arizona, a strategic move to potentially secure a state traditionally leaning Republican. Overall, by the end of September, Trump had spent about $190 million, while Clinton's spending totaled $401 million. Both Trump and Clinton can receive donations up to $5,400 from individual contributors, with the possibility of larger contributions that are divided between the campaign and joint fundraising efforts with national and state parties. Funds raised for national and state political parties are utilized for shared objectives such as hiring staff and mobilizing voters, but they cannot be directly applied to essential campaign functions like purchasing television ads or employing staff reporting directly to the campaign manager. Trump's campaign has faced difficulties in organizing and developing the necessary infrastructure to compete effectively in key battleground states, relying instead on the infrastructure established by the Republican Party. Trump has raised $244 million through joint fundraising committees with national parties, of which he received $71 million. In contrast, Clinton has raised $415 million through joint fundraisers, receiving $117 million for her campaign. Since 2008, major party presidential candidates have opted out of accepting public funding for general election campaigns, which imposed limits on the amounts candidates could raise and spend. However, the last candidate to accept public funds, Senator John McCain in 2008, raised more that year than Trump has this election, totaling over $300 million. That same year, Barack Obama raised $607 million in his first presidential campaign. In 2012, Mitt Romney raised over $337 million at the same point in the campaign, while Obama accumulated $564 million.

text: U.S. House Speaker Ryan offers election-year security agenda. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. House Speaker Paul Ryan introduced a national security policy emphasizing stronger defense on Thursday, as part of a conservative policy agenda aimed at unifying Republicans following a contentious primary campaign. The plan critiques President Barack Obama, attributing responsibility for “eight years of broken promises, concessions, and retreat” in the Syrian civil war, the nuclear deal with Iran, strained relations with Russia, and interactions with North Korea. It aims to reverse some of what Obama supporters consider his foreign policy successes, including the Iran deal and the approach toward normal relations with Cuba. The proposal also disapproves of attempts to close the Guantanamo detention center. While no specific figures are provided, it calls for an end to military rollbacks and insists on “adequate, predictable budgets.” The framework includes several deviations from foreign policy positions articulated by presumptive Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump, who has Ryan's endorsement for the White House race. It does not call for the construction of a large wall along the Mexican border, which is a key aspect of Trump’s campaign. Ryan advocates for border security measures that include “high fencing,” aerial surveillance, and radar. However, it aligns with some of Trump’s views regarding Muslim immigration, emphasizing the need to tighten refugee screening and exploring ways to prevent youth radicalization. Trump faced backlash for suggesting a temporary ban on Muslims entering the United States. “We must constantly reassess our defenses in order to find and close security gaps so that Islamist militants cannot slip into our country undetected,” the plan states. The proposal does not adopt an isolationist stance. It asserts a strong commitment to combating militants overseas, indicating that the United States must keep all options available and “eliminate terrorist sanctuaries.” Trump has critiqued certain U.S. alliances, while Ryan’s plan highlights the significance of NATO, describes relations with Israel as “the cornerstone of stability in the Middle East,” advocates stringent sanctions on Iran, and asserts that the United States should confront Russian aggression while supporting Ukraine. Additionally, it calls for more trade agreements and suggests that foreign aid programs should aim to make recipient countries self-sufficient. The plan also includes provisions for enhanced security for diplomats and facilities abroad. In this context, it references the 2012 attacks in Benghazi, which many Republicans utilize to question then-Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Trump’s opponent in the presidential race. Ryan, recognized as the highest-ranking elected Republican in the country, has characterized the agenda as a means to present voters with a coherent policy message for 2017. He introduced an anti-poverty agenda earlier in the week. Further initiatives on regulation, constitutional authority, healthcare, and tax reform are anticipated in the following weeks.

text: Death toll from fighting in South Sudan's Great Lakes rises to 170. JUBA (Reuters) - The death toll from inter-clan fighting in South Sudan's Great Lakes region last week has reached at least 170, according to officials on Tuesday. The clashes in Malek county occurred after a group of young men from the Ruop ethnic group attacked rival youth from the Pakam group on Wednesday and Thursday. Revenge attacks have subsequently taken place. Dharuai Mabor Teny, a member of parliament from the region, provided an updated death toll from the earlier count of 45. "Right now, from both sides, we have 170 plus people who lost their lives. 342 houses have been burnt and almost 1,800 people displaced," Teny told Reuters. The violence led the government to declare a three-month state of emergency in the region and surrounding areas on Monday. The military has been ordered to deploy troops to address the unrest. Shadrack Bol Maachok, the regional government’s spokesman, noted that the widespread availability of arms has complicated efforts to manage the conflict. "Those arms in the hands of the civilians are going to be taken away and heavy forces are going to be brought here," he told Reuters. The UN mission in South Sudan, UNMISS, stated that its troops were assisting in the removal of roadblocks erected by the clashing groups to facilitate movement and trade. South Sudan entered a state of war in 2013 following a political disagreement between President Salva Kiir and former vice president Riek Machar that escalated into military conflict. The fighting has resulted in tens of thousands of deaths, displaced about a quarter of the population of 12 million, and severely impacted the nation’s oil-dependent economy. Violence among rival communities is frequent in parts of South Sudan, often instigated by disputes over limited grazing land and cultural or political grievances.
